title: Yankees’ Gerrit Cole Ties CC Sabathia in MLB History
description: The New York Yankees made the call that folks weren’t sure they would make. Gerrit Cole is going to start Game 1 of the ALDS on Saturday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Despite struggles late in the season, Cole will get the ball for the game in Tropicana Field that could be crucial for the […] The post Yankees’ Gerrit Cole Ties CC Sabathia in MLB History appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The New York Yankees made the call that folks weren't sure they would make.

Gerrit Cole is going to start Game 1 of the ALDS on Saturday against the Tampa Bay Rays.

Despite struggles late in the season, Cole will get the ball for the game in Tropicana Field that could be crucial for the Yankees to win in what is just a best-of-five series.

The Cole Train comes to Tampa for ALDS Game 1 🚂#RepBX pic.twitter.com/uTSBdY0ba3

— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 2, 2026

Whether or not the Yankees should be starting Cole will only reveal itself on Saturday.

For now, there is a cool bit of history.

Cole has a long history of starting Game 1 in postseason series.

This will be his ninth Game 1 start (if you also include the single-game Wild Card Series that used to exist).

That's tied for fifth-most all-time, according to MLB Network's Sarah Langs.

Tied with Cole with nine of these starts? CC Sabathia.

In fourth place on the all-time Game 1 starts list is Greg Maddux, who had 11.

There's a tie for second place: Both Clayton Kershaw and Jon Lester started 12 of these games.

And alone in first place, potentially for a long time: Justin Verlander, with 14.

This will be the 9th time Gerrit Cole starts Game 1 of a postseason series (including singular Wild Card Game), tying CC Sabathia for 5th-most all time, behind:

Justin Verlander: 14
 Jon Lester: 12
 Clayton Kershaw: 12
 Greg Maddux: 11 https://t.co/NgopsVMhCQ

— Sarah Langs (@SlangsOnSports) October 2, 2026

Cole finished the 2026 regular season with a 3.61 ERA. That's his worst mark since 2017.

To be fair, it's still a really quality number, but Cole did prove a bit homer-prone late in the year. He also had his lowest strikeout rate (9.3 per nine innings) since that 2017 season, as well.

Cole has been a great playoff pitcher in his career. He has a 2.77 ERA in the postseason.

In the Yankees' 2024 playoff run to the World Series, he had a 2.17 ERA in five games.

Cole's most recent Game 1 start was in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series. He allowed just one run in six innings.

Cole has once faced the Rays in an ALDS Game 1, as well. That was in 2020. He went 6.0 innings and allowed three runs, including two home runs — Randy Arozarena with the first one, and Ji-man Choi with the second.

That game clearly has no real bearing on what happens on Saturday. The Rays beat the Yankees for the AL East title. Now, the Yanks will try and avenge that by potentially winning the ALDS. Cole will have to set the tone on the mound.

title: MLB insider says Phillies' Don Mattingly will be 'gracefully dismissed' as manager ending stint
description: The Philadelphia Phillies have made their decision with Don Mattingly it seems. The hunt for Alex Cora will likely begin soon.
fullText:
MLB insider says Phillies' Don Mattingly will be 'gracefully dismissed' as manager ending stint originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Philadelphia Phillies watched their season come to an end against the Atlanta Braves on Thursday night, which marked the first time they were beaten by their rival in the playoffs. The Phillies had an up-and-down year, to say the least.

The most notable development was the organization deciding to fire Rob Thomson after a brutal start to the year.

"There's a major shakeup in Philadelphia. The Phillies fired manager Rob Thomson on Tuesday morning. Don Mattingly is the interim skipper, with the team's press release saying he'll hold that position for the remainder of the 2026 season," MLB Trade Rumors' Anthony Franco wrote.

As the season went on, it was unclear what was going to happen with Don Mattingly. It seemed pretty obvious, though, that Mattingly was going to have to do a lot to remain the manager. USA Today's Bob Nightengale believed it was going to take a World Series appearance to bring him back.

"Philadelphia Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly, who took over for Rob Thomson on April 28, not only must lead the Phillies to the postseason, but likely to the World Series or even win it to be asked back. Alex Cora, who turned down the job when Thomson was fired, is expected to be the Phillies' next manager barring a World Series berth or title," Nightengale wrote.

With the season coming to an end on Thursday night, all eyes are turned toward Mattingly and his future. Nightengale reported that a graceful dismissal will be coming.

"Mattingly, who managed the Phillies for five months, will be gracefully dismissed, likely in the coming week. The Phillies will announce the decision as a mutual parting, and will offer Mattingly the chance to stay in the organization, perhaps as an advisor, where his son, Preston, is the GM under Dave Dombrowski, president of baseball operations," Nightengale wrote.

Dombrowski's connection to Alex Cora has been apparent from the beginning, but Mattingly is still going to be involved with the organization. The Phillies are going to look like a whole new team next season, including at the manager spot.

It was a good run from Mattingly, as he helped turn the season around for the Phillies. Now, it is just a matter of when he is going to be officially let go by Philadelphia, and it will be very soon.

title: 'Deeply unwelcome': MLB backs off its plan for a game at Grand Teton
description: The Grand Teton national park in Wyoming.Photograph: Ronen...
fullText:
Major League Baseball (MLB) leadership is no longer considering holding a game inside a national park, according to a letter commissioner Robert Manfred sent to officials in Teton county, Wyoming, on Thursday in what could be the league's biggest swing-and-a-miss off the diamond.

On 26 September, the Washington Post reported that MLB had reached out to the White House about staging a one-day game at Grand Teton national park in Wyoming. Teton county describes itself as a "a year-round resort community" and sits within the Jackson Hole valley. It's also a habitat for grizzly bears, osprey, bison and more.

News of MLB's outreach to the federal government quickly sparked concern about the impact that erecting a field and the infrastructure to hold spectators could have on the natural landscape and habitat of scores of wildlife that call the 310,000-acre (125,500-hectare) park home.

In the letter, Manfred noted that MLB had held games at places like the Fort Bragg military base in North Carolina and the nation's oldest Negro Leagues stadium in Birmingham, Alabama. He added that MLB staff had been doing their due diligence to see whether a game at Grand Teton was possible and to evaluate the potential environmental impact.

"Since the story was reported, it has become clear that the local community does not want us to continue Grand Teton national park as a potential site," Manfred wrote.

The outrage over the possible MLB game comes as national parks across the US struggle under funding cuts, staffing shortages and consistent overcrowding.

A Teton county commissioner, Luther Propst, who described the potential game as an "incomprehensible and deeply unwelcome notion", celebrated the MLB's decision in a post on Facebook.

"Ever since I got a call from the Washington Post about [MLB] scouting a ballfield in Grand Teton National Park, I have been hoping this idea would die a quick death – and today it did!" he wrote. "This is what can happen when we stand up firmly together, and I am proud to have played my part."

In a statement to the Guardian, a White House spokesperson said that it was approached by the MLB about the possibility of hosting the game but the National Park Service had not granted any permits to do so and the game is not a White House directive.

Neither MLB nor the National Park Service immediately responded to the Guardian's request for comment.

title: Seven MLB players who played all 162 games in 2026
description: Every spring, dozens of players say they want to play every day. By the final Sunday of the 2026 regular season, only seven had actually done it, appearing in all 162 of their team’s games. The group mixes a record-chasing first baseman, a two-time MVP, a rookie and an MVP front-runner. Each took a different…
fullText:
Every spring, dozens of players say they want to play every day. By the final Sunday of the 2026 regular season, only seven had actually done it, appearing in all 162 of their team's games.

The group mixes a record-chasing first baseman, a two-time MVP, a rookie and an MVP front-runner. Each took a different path to the same number, and several got there for the first time in their careers.

Modern teams lean heavily on scheduled rest days, platoons and cautious injury management. That makes a full-season line on the stat sheet a rare badge, one that reflects health, trust from managers and a little luck.

Luck cut the other way for Baltimore's Pete Alonso. He played in 161 games, but the Orioles' Sept. 27 finale at Yankee Stadium was canceled by weather after a nearly three-hour delay, leaving no 162nd game to play.

Alonso still finished with an AL-leading 43 home runs and 113 RBIs. The seven who made it, however, start with a player who has turned showing up into a historic habit.

Atlanta's Matt Olson played every game for the fifth straight season. His consecutive games streak, which began May 2, 2021, with the Oakland Athletics, reached 944 games by the end of the year, according to The Associated Press.

That total pushes Olson past Stan Musial's 895 on the all-time list. On July 10, he also passed Dale Murphy for the longest streak in Braves franchise history, with his 741st straight game for Atlanta.

Olson has never treated the streak as a goal. "I just expect to play if I'm healthy and ready to go, and it's just kind of stacked up games," he told MLB.com after setting the franchise mark.

Two-time MVP Bryce Harper appeared in all 162 games for the first time in his 15-season MLB career. His previous high was 159 games with Washington in 2018. Before 2026, his only Philadelphia season above 145 games was 2019, when he played 157.

The 33-year-old Phillies star had spoken openly about his goal. "Obviously, it's in my head that I want to do it," Harper said in July, while emphasizing the importance of staying healthy and winning.

His final regular-season appearance carried playoff stakes. Harper homered in Philadelphia's 7-3 victory over Tampa Bay on September 27, clinching the final NL wild-card berth with an 88-74 record.

Matt Olson had company in the Braves' lineup throughout the regular season. Second baseman Ozzie Albies also appeared in all 162 games, a notable turnaround after injuries interrupted several recent seasons.

Albies broke his left foot in 2022 and fractured his left wrist in 2024, missing substantial time in both years. In 2026, he stayed on the field as Atlanta finished 94-68 and won the NL East.

The Braves improved by 18 wins over 2025, with their durable infielders providing a steady foundation. Atlanta opened its Wild Card Series against Philadelphia with a 5-3 victory on September 29.

On the other side of that game stood Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero, who made history of his own. He became just the fourth player since divisional play began in 1969 to start all 162 games at third base.

Caminero joined Sal Bando in 1969, Cal Ripken Jr. in 1997 and Vinny Castilla in 1998. Few positions are more physically demanding over a full season, which helps explain why the list is so short.

The 23-year-old paired that durability with production. He reached 40 home runs with a September walk-off that clinched a playoff berth and topped 100 RBIs for a second straight season on a 98-win Rays club.

Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong also played in all 162 games, and his season may carry the biggest award implications of the group. He is widely considered a leading candidate for NL MVP honors.

Crow-Armstrong tied Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead with 45 home runs, according to MLB.com's final stat leaders. He also led the NL with a .942 OPS and topped the majors with 10.6 WAR.

Earlier this season, he became only the second left-handed hitter in Cubs history to hit 40 home runs in a season, joining Hall of Famer Billy Williams. Doing it without a day off only adds to the case.

Cincinnati's Sal Stewart became the first rookie to appear in all 162 games since Delmon Young did it for Tampa Bay in 2007. Stewart started 161 games and made 1 appearance as a pinch-hitter.

He stayed in the lineup while playing first base, second base, and third base and also serving as a designated hitter. Stewart finished with 32 home runs and a Reds rookie record 111 RBIs.

The 22-year-old earned an All-Star selection during his rookie season. "I'm blessed. I had a great year, but I'm not satisfied," Stewart said, according to Sports Illustrated.

Pittsburgh's Bryan Reynolds became the first Pirates player to appear in all 162 games since Jason Bay in 2005.

Reynolds had approached that mark before, playing 159 games in 2021 and 156 in 2024. In 2026, he combined his durability with steady production, finishing with a major league-leading 40 doubles.

Pirates manager Don Kelly praised Reynolds's stability and consistency. Reynolds joined 6 other players in reaching 162 appearances during the regular season, earning a distinction that remains rare.

Fun fact: Olson's 944-game streak is impressive, but it's still well short of the record. Cal Ripken Jr. played in 2,632 consecutive games, the longest streak in MLB history.

Seven players appeared in all 162 games in 2026: Matt Olson, Ozzie Albies, Bryce Harper, Junior Caminero, Pete Crow-Armstrong, Sal Stewart, and Bryan Reynolds.

Olson's streak reached 944 games, passing Stan Musial on the all-time list.

Harper, Reynolds, and Albies reached 162 games for the first time.

Caminero became the fourth player since 1969 to start all 162 games at third base.

Stewart was the first rookie to play every game since 2007.

Pete Alonso played 161 after a rainout wiped out Baltimore's finale.

title: Former Braves Closer, 2-Time All-Star And MLB Saves Leader Ends Career With 3 Words
description: The Atlanta Braves got a retirement update from a former star who suddenly announced the end of his career on the last day of the season.
fullText:
The Atlanta Braves are preparing for another postseason run with one of their most important bullpen reinforcements finally nearing full strength.

Robert Suarez, who missed several months with an elbow injury, has returned to action at a crucial time as Atlanta prepares to face the rival Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card round.

"The Braves bullpen was one of the best in baseball even without set-up man Robert Suarez for three months," Jesus Cano reported for The Athletic. "But they were glad to see him make two appearances since returning from right elbow inflammation this past week."

Suarez's return gives Atlanta another high-leverage option alongside Raisel Iglesias and the rest of a deep relief corps. He posted a 0.56 ERA across his first 31 appearances before his elbow issue sidelined him in June.

But alongside the news of Suarez's imminent return, the Braves also received an update on a former centerpiece of their bullpen at the end of the regular season. Kirby Yates, who spent the 2022 and 2023 seasons in Atlanta, announced that his playing career is officially over.

Cubs Castoff Cut By New Team Immediately After Disastrous Outing

Yates confirmed his retirement decision publicly after making the first start of his 12-year MLB career for the Pittsburgh Pirates on Saturday, pitching one and two-thirds scoreless innings against the Detroit Tigers. The appearance was also part of a memorable final day for Justin Verlander, who was making his final MLB appearance for Detroit.

"This is it," Yates announced in a postgame interview with SportsNet Pittsburgh. "I just didn't really want to say anything, publicly, until the end."

That three-word message delivered a clear answer after Yates hinted at the idea of ending his career leading up to the final appearance.

Yates leaves baseball as a two-time All-Star and the 2019 National League saves leader. That season with the San Diego Padres produced 41 saves and a 1.19 ERA, establishing the right-hander as one of baseball's premier closers. He later earned his second All-Star selection with the Texas Rangers in 2024 after recording 33 saves and a 1.17 ERA.

Yankees Legend Quickly Deletes Jab At CC Sabathia Monument Park Decision

Yates originally joined the Braves on a two-year, $8.25 million contract before the 2022 season. His first year in Atlanta followed an extended recovery from elbow surgery, but he returned to become a reliable bullpen piece and posted a 3.28 ERA across 60 and one-third innings in 2023.

His career ultimately included stops with eight MLB organizations, 518 appearances, 101 saves and a 3.35 ERA. He also overcame the unusual path of reaching the majors after going undrafted out of junior college.

"I don't have anything left, let's put it that way," Yates told SportsNet Pittsburgh. "I've been running on fumes here for a while… I've given this game everything I have and in return it's given me more than I could ever thank it for or imagine."

For many Braves fans, Yates' retirement announcement will recall some big moments in the recent past, including his only postseason appearance, which came in the 2023 National League Division Series against the Phillies. As the Braves once again prepare to face their division rival in the playoffs, fans will take a moment to remember the former bullpen piece as a long and successful career comes to an end.

title: Astros weren't great in regular season, but neither were these teams that reached World Series
description: The Astros are the first team with a .500 record to make the MLB postseason. They can look this list of teams who also underachieved in the regular season, but got hot at the right time.
fullText:
You know what they call a team with a mediocre regular season record that gets hot at the right time and wins the World Series? Champions.

That's all the Houston Astros care about as they enter the postseason with the distinction of being the sport's playoff-qualifier with the fewest wins in a complete 162-game schedule.

Still, they're in the postseason, which means, beginning with Tuesday's start of the wild-card series against the Chicago White Sox, they're 14 victories away from winning a World Series that brings with it a banner that will fly just as high and a trophy that will shine just as bright as the other two in franchise history.

If the Astros need any encouragement, they can look at history and find plenty of teams who had discouraging regular seasons, but found their stride in October and went all the way to the World Series.

Here are the teams with the worst regular seasons that still made it to the end…

Lost World Series
Before the current version of the Astros came along, the Mets and the 2005 San Diego Padres owned the record for playoff teams with the fewest wins in a full regular season. Unlike the Padres, the Mets, led by 1973 Cy Young Award winner Tom Seaver and managed by Yogi Berra, made it all the way to the World Series. The Mets, who became known for Tug McGraw's catchphrase "Ya Gotta Believe!!!", were in last place with a month to play and five games below .500 on Sept. 11 before winning 12 of their final 16 games. They beat the vaunted Big Red Machine of the Cincinnati Reds in the NLCS and had a 3-2 series lead on the Oakland Athletics before dropping Games 6 and 7 to lose the World Series.

Won World Series
The Cardinals, whose .516 winning percentage is the lowest for any World Series champion, had two separate eight-game losing streaks - by comparison, the Astros lost eight in a row once in April - and a seven-game losing streak, but still outpaced the Astros by 1 ½ games in a weak National League Central. They went on to shock the San Diego Padres in the NLDS and take out the New York Mets in a seven-game NLCS before coasting past Justin Verlander and the Detroit Tigers in just five games in the World Series. The light-hitting David Eckstein was named World Series MVP for hitting .364 against the Tigers.

Lost World Series
The Diamondbacks narrowly earned a wild-card spot despite getting swept by the Astros in the regular season's final series, which the Astros needed to edge out the Texas Rangers in the AL West. Arizona upset the Brewers in the wild-card series, then swept the Dodgers in the NLDS despite finishing 16 games behind them in the NL West. The Diamondbacks, who were led offensively by current Astros first baseman Christian Walker, needed seven games to beat the Phillies in the NLCS before finally succumbing to the Rangers, who had eliminated the Astros in a tense seven-game ALCS.

Won World Series
Before the 2006 St. Louis Cardinals came along, this Twins team was the worst to win a World Series. The Kirby Puckett-led Twins went just 29-52 on the road in the regular season but used the raucous Metrodome to their advantage in the postseason, winning all four home games over the St. Louis Cardinals in the World Series. The Twins still are the only team with a losing run differential in the regular season to go on and win the World Series. The Twins were outscored by 20 runs in the regular season, while the current Astros were outscored by 32.

Won World Series
It's tough to think about any of those Yankees teams that three-peated from 1998-2000 as not great, but the last team of that title run limped to the finish, losing 15 of its final 18 games while still managing to hold off the Boston Red Sox for a playoff spot. Once the Yankees were in, though, they got hot and beat the Athletics in a thrilling five-game ALDS before finishing off the Mariners in six games in the ALCS. With Andy Pettitte and Roger Clemens leading the pitching staff, the Yankees crushed the Mets in a Subway World Series that included Clemens chunking a broken bat at Mets slugger Mike Piazza during Game 2.

Lost World Series
Cleveland was the beneficiary of playing in a weak American League Central where no other team finished above .500 that season. Still, Cleveland had a potent offense with Jim Thome, Matt Williams and David Justice each hitting more than 30 home runs. Cleveland went through the Yankees and Orioles in the playoffs before falling to the Florida Marlins in a thrilling seven-game World Series that ended with a walk-off single from Édgar Rentería.

Lost World Series
Astros fans all know what ultimately happened to this Phillies team, but it was a feat that it even made it this far. Philadelphia got off to such a poor start that manager Joe Girardi was fired in June. Under interim manager Rob Thomson, the Phillies went 65-46 the rest of the way to make the playoffs by one game. From there, they eliminated the Cardinals, Braves and Padres before running into the Astros, who had won 106 regular-season games and finished off Philadelphia in six games.

Won World Series
The 2014 World Series pitted two teams that didn't reach 90 wins in the regular season with the 89-73 Kansas City Royals falling to the 88-74 Giants. That Giants team didn't have much of an offense with no one one the team reaching 25 home runs or 90 RBIs, but it rode the arm of Madison Bumgarner in the postseason. Bumgarner, who threw a complete-game shutout in Game 5 of the World Series and came back to throw five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, pitched a remarkable seven times in that playoff run, putting up a 1.03 ERA in 52 ⅔ innings.

Won World Series
Astros fans are plenty familiar with this team. The Braves entered the postseason with the worst record of anyone in the playoffs that year. They were 5 games out in August, but went 36-18 over the final two months of the regular season and kept that hot streak going in the postseason, including beating the 95-win Astros in six games in the World Series. Jorge Soler, who hit a ball completely out of the Astros' home ballpark, was named World Series MVP.

There's more to Houston with the Chronicle.

title: These former Milwaukee Brewers will be suiting up in MLB playoffs
description: The 2026 MLB playoffs will feature a number of familiar faces for Milwaukee Brewers fans, including Freddy Peralta, Caleb Durbin and Josh Hader.
fullText:
The Milwaukee Brewers have the best record in baseball and the best record in club history, and their reward is a relaxing five days while the wild-card series play out, beginning Tuesday. Sept. 29.

Here's a look at former Brewers who will likely get a shot in the postseason:

The former Brewers star has been special again. He finished the year with a 1.01 ERA and 26 saves in 45 innings, with 55 strikeouts, just 15 walks, one home run allowed and an absurd 0.761 WHIP. At age 32, he's still doing some of his best work.

Traded in 2021 as part of the Willy Adames package, the multi-time all-star is one of the best pitchers in baseball, with a 2.67 ERA in 30 starts this year, 174 strikeouts in 172 innings and a 0.913 WHIP, the best among qualified American League starters.

Though the long-tenured Brewers star, traded this offseason to the New York Mets, initially struggled after his deadline trade to Tampa, he's been nails ever since.

In 55 innings with the Rays, he has a 3.25 ERA with a 1.012 WHIP. He's allowed just three earned runs in his last six starts (34 innings).

Traded in the offseason, Durbin posted a 4.4 WAR season according to Baseball Reference as the Red Sox third baseman, finishing with a .710 OPS, 13 homers and 20 steals.

If those numbers don't sound eye-popping enough to register such a high WAR number (101 OPS-plus indicates he's just slightly above average), consider that Fielding Bible and Statcast both rank him as the best third baseman in the American League (13 Defensive Runs Saved and seven Outs Above Average).

He's been a key part of Boston's surge from early season malaise to clear-cut wild-card team in the American League.

Another player who went to Boston with Durbin in the deal that brought three contributors to Milwaukee, Monasterio only had a .665 OPS and six homers in 107 games, but he provided the same versatility in Boston (games at every infield position) that he did in Milwaukee.

Anthony Seigler, the third person in that deal, played in 49 games this year but closed the year on the injured list with wrist inflammation. He's taking ground balls again, but it's unclear if he'll be available for the postseason. Seigler had a .727 OPS.

It's unclear if Grisham will make the wild-card roster after he missed most of September with a right hamstring injury, although he has said he's ready to play.

The Brewers' first-round draft pick in 2015 and breakout rookie in 2019 spent his third season in New York, and his numbers declined after a huge 2025 (34 homers, .811 OPS) with 18 homers and a .703 OPS this season in 121 games.

His defense has also been below-average the past couple of years, according to the DRS and OAA metrics.

The former Milwaukee left-hander had a quality season in the Sox bullpen, posting a 3.74 ERA in 61 innings, with a 1.27 WHIP. Hudson had a 1.73 ERA in the Brewers bullpen in 2024.

He made 15 starts and had a strong 3.83 ERA in 141 innings this year with the White Sox. He pitched in just seven games last year for the Brewers after the team picked him up late in the year, with a 3.38 ERA.

The reliever posted a 3.78 ERA in 52 games and 79 innings, with a quality WHIP of 1.13.

Richards had a 3.20 ERA in 2021, acquired from Tampa Bay in the Adames trade and then sent to Toronto in the Rowdy Tellez trade.

Since pitching in Milwaukee, he's made big-league appearances for the Blue Jays, Twins, Royals, Diamondbacks, Phillies and now White Sox.

A Brewer the last two seasons, Hoskins gets an extra week to rest the back inflammation that has had him on the injured list since Aug. 19, but it's unclear if he'll be available when the Guardians begin ALDS play.

He's batting just .179 this year with a .682 OPS (13 homers in 95 games).

He wasn't a Brewer for long, traded in 2019 for Drew Pomeranz, but his career has continued quite nicely. He had a .719 OPS this year and 12 homers for Atlanta, both increases over his last couple years with Houston.

More importantly, he can play outfield or infield defense, and he's got two career Gold Gloves to show for it.

The popular ex-Brewers left-hander was dealt from the Angels at the deadline and was excellent in Atlanta, posting a 1.63 ERA in 28 innings of work. He allowed just one home run and had a WHIP of 0.882.

He appeared in three games for the Brewers in 2024 and appeared in 20 for the Braves and finished the regular season on the Atlanta roster.

He had 10 hits, including five doubles, during his 47 plate appearances, and he's capable of playing multiple outfield spots. With Lane Thomas injured, there's a real chance he gets a playoff roster spot.

Sent from the Mets to the Cubs before the deadline, the outfielder has been excellent, with an .890 OPS in 82 plate appearances.

The longtime ex-Brewer was in the organization beginning in 2012 and on the big-league roster from 2019 to 2023. He played with the Mets against the Brewers in the 2024 postseason.

He made 19 starts for the Cubs this year and appeared in 34 games overall, recording a 4.34 ERA in 137 innings (101 strikeouts, 1.328 WHIP). The Brewers pitcher in 2021, 2023 and 2024 was with the Cubs last year when they faced Milwaukee in the playoffs.

Civale, who faced the Brewers in the 2025 playoffs, had another great year for the Cubs in limited work, with a 1.72 ERA in 18 games and a 1.064 WHIP. He's not a lock to make this year's postseason roster, but don't count him out.

Jahmai Jones, Boston Red Sox. Briefly a Brewer in 2023 and then a Tiger for all of last year, he was acquired midseason and was amazing for Boston in 37 games, posting a .993 OPS with four homers and four doubles in 76 plate appearances.

Tristan Peters, Chicago White Sox. Never a Brewer but a member of the Brewers farm system and famously traded for Trevor Rosenthal in 2022, a pitcher who never appeared for the Brewers. Peters was an all-star this year and finished with 3.6 WAR, playing center field and posting a .774 OPS (12 homers, eight steals, 56 RBIs). It was a true breakout season for the 26-year-old.

Daulton Varsho, Houston Astros. The native of Marshfield (never a Brewer) appeared in the World Series last year with Toronto and was acquired at the deadline by the Astros, but he had to be placed on the injured list with wrist inflammation and may not be available in the playoffs.

Bennett Sousa, Houston Astros. He appeared in 35 games out of the bullpen for Houston and had a 6.00 ERA. He pitched in two games for Milwaukee in 2023.

AJ Blubaugh, Houston Astros. Not a Brewer, but the UW-Milwaukee alumnus had an excellent year in the bullpen, posting a 3.66 ERA in 64 games and 96 innings, with 94 strikeouts and a 1.23 WHIP.

David Fry, Cleveland Guardians. The former Brewers minor-leaguer, traded in an ill-fated deal for reliever JC Mejía, had a .677 OPS in 91 games this year, a far cry from his all-star campaign of two years ago.

Craig Yoho, Cleveland Guardians. He's flashed some of the same high-level potential that he did with the Brewers before getting traded before the deadline in the deal that brought Bo Naylor to Milwaukee. But Yoho has also been prone to blowups, including one Sept. 26 that might have been the last straw for his hopes of appearing on the playoff roster. He ended the season off the roster, getting demoted before the season finale. Yoho had a 6.87 ERA in 19 games with Cleveland.

Alex Call, Los Angeles Dodgers. Not a Brewer, but the River Falls native won a ring last year and has appeared in 88 games for the Dodgers this season, playing primarily left field, with a .655 OPS. It's unclear if he and backup catcher Ben Rortvedt (from Verona) will have a place on the postseason roster.

Drake Baldwin, Atlanta Braves. The Madison West alumnus and 2025 Rookie of the Year had a great follow-up in 2026, starting the All-Star Game and finishing with 25 homers and an .817 OPS.

Elieser Hernández, Atlanta Braves. He was a Brewer for just four games in 2024 and has bounced around a lot, but he did have a 2.25 ERA in five games for the Braves and finished the season on the active roster.

Luis Rengifo, San Diego Padres. The infielder struggled with Milwaukee in 2026 and famously hit more home runs against the Brewers (a grand slam) than with them (zero homers before he was released), part of his revitalization in San Diego (.784 OPS). But he was lost for the season when he tore his ACL and MCL in late August.

title: Season Ends for Rockies With Loss to White Sox
description: The Colorado Rockies wrapped up the 2026 MLB season as the postseason-bound Chicago White Sox secured a victory.
fullText:
The 2026 MLB season came to an end for the Colorado Rockies on Sunday afternoon and, unfortunately, it ended with a loss.

Colorado finished its season with a 58-104 season record. It was not the season that the Rockies, players, or fans wanted to see happen. Yes, there were some things that were good to look at and others, well, not so much.

On Sunday at Rate Field in Chicago, the Chicago White Sox defeated Colorado 4-2. Kyle Freeland got the start for Colorado and he took the loss. His season record ends up at 4-12, going four innings and giving up seven hits, four earned runs, no walks, two strikeouts, and surrendering two home runs.

Mark Manfredi, Nick Frasso, and Jaden Hill came out of the Rockies' bullpen to put the stops to a Chicago offense that took control of this series.

Connor Norby's sacrifice fly in the top of the third inning set Colorado up with an early 1-0 lead. Chicago, though, bounced right back with a four-run third and took a 4-1 advantage.

Cole Carrigg, who had a heck of a season, put the Rockies' final run on the board this season with his 13th home run in the top of the eighth inning.

The Rockies were 0-for-2 with runners in scoring position and left four total runners on base. As for the White Sox, they were 2-for-10 with runners in scoring position and left six total runners on base.

Norby, Carrigg, Kyle Karros, Adael Amador, and Jordan Beck were the only hitters for Colorado to get base hits in Game No. 162.

Let's break down what the 104 losses mean for the Rockies this season. They are tied for the second-most in franchise history along with the 2023 Rockies, but the team also had a 15-loss improvement over last season's team that finished 43-119.

Yes, this is the fourth straight season that the Rockies have lost 100-plus games. In 2024, Colorado was 61-101 and the 2023 Rockies were 59-103. This season's squad finished up going 3-17 in its last 20 games going back to Sept. 6. Now, since Aug. 17, Colorado finished up 8-30.

Those are hard numbers to look at for a franchise looking to turn things around. Some of the Rockies' young players in the Pacific Coast League earned recognition, so there might be some hope of future help.

What does the future, though, look like for the pitching situation? That will be worth keeping an eye on in the offseason.

For now, Rockies fans, this season is over. A lockout looms over the start of the 2027 MLB season. If that's avoidable, then Spring Training will come around before you know it.

title: Giants manager Tony Vitello ends rough first season with MLB-high seventh ejection
description: The Giants took a big step backward in their first year under the former college coach.
fullText:
Tony Vitello's first season as an MLB manager ended a few innings earlier than expected.

The San Francisco Giants manager was ejected in the third inning of his team's season finale against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday, responding irately to a check-swing call from first-base umpire Marvin Hudson. Hudson gave Vitello a quick boot, prompting Vitello to get his money's worth.

It was Vitello's seventh ejection this season, the most by any manager in MLB and the most by an National League manager since then-Cincinnati Reds manager David Bell's seven in 2023.

Tony Vitello has been ejected after arguing this check-swing call 🤬 pic.twitter.com/XcobZmbhA3

Vitello and the Giants did appear to have a point. With a 2-2 count, one out and runners on first and second, Dodgers star Mookie Betts' bat clearly went past the plate on a high fastball from Sam Hentges. It should have been strike 3, which Hentges got one pitch later on a swinging strike on another high fastball.

Check swing calls are explicitly a judgement call for umpires and are not reviewable. They are also a bit of a sore spot for the Giants in games against the Dodgers, as a 107-win Giants team had its season ended in the 2021 NLDS against the Dodgers when the umpires ruled Wilmer Flores swung at a pitch.

Vitello wasn't the manager for that game. He joined the Giants last offseason as one of MLB's most outside-the-box managerial hires in recent memory. Before 2026, Vitello had never worked in professional baseball, not even as a minor-league player. Giants president of baseball operations Buster Posey made the hire after Vitello's successful tenure as head coach at Tennessee, with the Volunteers winning the College World Series in 2024.

The Giants tasked Vitello with steering a veteran roster looking to make the playoffs for the first time since that 2021 checked-swing call. Instead, they took a massive step backwards, with the club going from an 81-81 record in 2025 under veteran MLB manager Bob Melvin to a 65-96 record under Vitello entering Sunday. They would be in last place in any other division save the historically awful AL West.

That under-performance isn't entirely Vitello's fault. An aged roster was beset by injuries, with Rafael Devers, Willy Adames, Matt Chapman, Jung Hoo Lee, Harrison Bader, Logan Webb and many more on the injured list as of Sunday, to say nothing of certain players' underperformance.

That said, Vitello also didn't exactly impress observers. The team got off to a bad start with a number of clubhouse incidents and never recovered. Vitello also caught significant flack for his handling, or lack thereof, of the Giants' Pride Night incident in June.

Vitello was a risky bet for Posey, whose own tenure hasn't been sparkling since he replaced Farhan Zaidi in 2024, which was a significant philosophical shift for the Giants. It's enough for Vitello to be considered on the hot seat for 2027, if he isn't there already.

title: Why 60 games is magic number in MLB's imminent lockout | Nightengale's Nobteook
description: MLB is heading for a lockout that could last months into the 2027 season.
fullText:
A growing number of executives believe that the 2027 Major League Baseball season will begin around Memorial Day weekend next year considering that if 60 or more games are cancelled next season, players will miss about four paychecks and national TV contracts would be extended through 2029.

The collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, with the league demanding a hard salary cap and that idea being an absolute non-starter for the players.

The 2021-22 lockout was the longest in history at 99 days, but the two sides agreed on a deal that preserved a full 162-game season.

– While manager Dan Wilson will be blamed for the Seattle Mariners' embarrassing season and is expected to pay the price by being fired as early as Monday, Jerry Dipoto, the Mariners' president of baseball operations, is under heavy scrutiny.

Dipoto doesn't appear to be in jeopardy of being fired, but critics point out that the Mariners have reached the postseason just twice in his 11-year tenure, and veteran catcher Cal Raleigh went public about the Mariners' cultural woes .

"I think it was a collective failure, unfortunately,'' Raleigh told reporters. "It's going to take a lot of people having some self-reflection, myself included, on the direction of where we're heading, what we want to be, and who we want to be as a team. What is our team identity? I don't feel like there was one this year….''

The Mariners have plenty of disgruntled employees, with everyone from assistant GMs to equipment managers to strength and conditioning coaches being fired in recent years. And if the Mariners don't reach the postseason next year, those fingers will be pointed directly at Dipoto.

– Former Texas Rangers GM Jon Daniels, who guided the Rangers to back-to-back pennants, pulled himself out of consideration for the Athletics' GM vacancy for family reasons. Daniels, who has two kids in college and one in high school, was flattered by the opportunity, but enjoys his job as a senior advisor in baseball operations for the Tampa Bay Rays.

– The easy solution to avoid another Alex Bregman incident (suffering facial fractures when hit by a foul ball getting ready to hit), MLB executives say, is for the hitter in the on-deck circle to stand on the same side the batter is hitting. So, if Bregman had been standing on the other side of the field from left-handed hitting Michael Busch, the accident could have been prevented.

– The World Baseball Classic took a massive hit this week when 2025 Cy Young winner Paul Skenes blamed his participation in this year's WBC for his massive struggles, with San Francisco Giants ace Logan Webb also suffering his worst season.

Skenes threw 75 pitches at 95-mph or faster during the WBC, topping out at 99.7-mph. He didn't reach that velocity the entire season, with his fastball down 2-mph from his rookie season in 2024.

"It definitely affected the year," Skenes told reporters. "Unfortunately, I don't think I'm the only one."

The WBC is scheduled to resume in 2030, two years after the Olympics, but GMs are hoping that MLB could change the format to have at least the final rounds played during the All-Star break, to avoid the rash of pitching injuries when arms simply aren't ready in March.

– Dave Dombrowski, Phillies president of baseball operations, preaches the importance of veteran clubhouse leadership, believing it's essential for teams with postseason aspirations.

"I think veteran leadership is extremely important," Dombrowski tells USA TODAY Sports. "Not everybody necessarily agrees with this, but veteran leadership on what it takes to win."

Dombrowski has leaders Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in Philadelphia, had Dustin Pedroia and Mookie Betts in Boston, Victor Martinez, Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander in Detroit, and insists they wouldn't have won the 1997 World Series without Darren Daulton and Craig Counsell in Florida.

– What a storybook ending to Justin Verlander's Hall of Fame career, not only showing flashes of his greatness in his final outing, but having his 7-year-old daughter wearing a Tigers jersey with her dad's name and number, running to the mound to hug him after being lifted from the game. Verlander stood on the mound sobbing.

"That hit me,'' Verlander said, "like a ton of bricks."

– San Diego Padres catcher Ethan Salas, 20 years, 116 days, who was not old enough to drink during the Padres' clinching celebration, so the Padres gave him a bucket containing apple cider, baby bottles and a tiny jersey with a letterboard that read: BABY'S FIRST CLINCHMAS.

Salas will be the youngest catcher in baseball history to participate in the postseason.

– Hall of Fame shortstop Barry Larkin raised some eyebrows when he criticized the Reds' front office in his final broadcast, which drew strong support from former Reds All-Star MVP Joey Votto

"I think these last three weeks of baseball playing against some of the better teams that are going to be going to the postseason really illustrate how far we are behind at this big-league level," Larkin said. "Change has to happen. This city deserves better than that, and I know every player down there feels that. But something has to give. We have to get better because we are so, so far behind.''

The ownership group announced that GM Nick Krall and his staff are returning for 2027.

– It's hard to believe that with more than 125 years of co-existence, this will be only the fourth postseason that the Cubs and White Sox have played in together, and they clinched their postseason berths just two minutes apart on Thursday.

– Miami Marlins Gold Glove infielder Javier Sanoja has had a surreal year. It began when he scored the winning run for Venezuela in their WBC championship game, and continued through the season, hitting  .294, including a league-leading .339 since Aug. 1. He's also the only National League position player to play in 10 or more games at five different positions this season (22 games at second, 117 at third, 10 at shortstop, 10 in left field and 14 in right field).

The highlight, though, Sanoja tells USA TODAY Sports, will always be winning the gold medal for his country.

"It meant so much for our country, and our people who are such big fans of the game," Sanoja said. "Every city I go, someone in the stands is congratulating me for the championship. It fills me with a lot of emotion. It's a night I'll never forget as long as I live."

– There's just something about September that brings out the best in the Guardians. They have won eight of their last nine games entering Saturday, and are 83-48 in September since the 2022 season_second-best in the AL behind only the Yankees.

– The Chicago White Sox, who grabbed Luis Castillo at the trade deadline, need to find a way to fix him in 2027 or else they just wasted $20 million. He was an albatross on their staff since his acquisition, going 1-2 with an 8.42 ERA in nine appearances.

– You can expect Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle to be a key to their hopes of defeating the Yankees in the wild-card round. Tolle now only has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts, but he has given up just one run and four hits in 13 innings with 18 strikeouts in his two starts against the Yankees this year.

– The Guardians are the first team to reach the postseason without a single qualifying player hitting .300 or hitting 20 homers or driving in 75 runs or stealing 40 bases, according to OptaSTATS.

– Randal Grichuk, who was released by the Yankees and signed a $1.25 million contract, has been an absolute godsend for the White Sox.

Grichuk signed with the White Sox on May 4 after Austin Hays suffered a left calf strain, and has hit .304 with 14 homers and 41 RBIs for the Sox, slashing .400/.408/.733 with four doubles, three home runs and nine RBIs in his last 15 games entering Saturday.

"He's obviously responded to the opportunity here, taking advantage of it," White Sox manager Will Venable told reporters. "He's been as good as anybody in this league offensively."

– Former Diamondbacks owner Jerry Colangelo, who led his franchise to its 2001 World Series title, was not part of the 25-year reunion celebration last week but plans to have his own dinner party for the team and staff in November.

– If the Pittsburgh Pirates want to be taken seriously, they do everything possible to bring back Brandon Lowe, who's a free agent this winter. Lowe has hit 33 home runs, the most by a Pirates' player since Josh Bell in 2019, with his 19 homers at PNC Park the most in the ballpark's history.

– The Yankees cringe watching Ezequiel Durán with the Texas Rangers. They traded him at the 2021 trade deadline for outfielder Joey Gallo.

– This is the Astros' worst season since 2014. ... and yet may win the AL West with a losing record.

– The Arizona Diamondbacks can't thank the St. Louis Cardinals enough for giving them Nolan Arenado this winter. The Diamondbacks not only had the Cardinals pay all but $11 million of the remaining $42 million that Arenado is owed, but Arenado has carried the D-backs' offense, hitting a team-leading 30 homers with 85 RBI and a .803 OPS, his best season since 2022. Arenado joins Hall of Famers Eddie Mathews and Mike Schmidt as the only third basemen in MLB history to have eight 30-homer seasons.

And the D-backs got Arenado for the mere cost of mid-level prospect Jack Martinez.

– How much does Aaron Judge mean to the Yankees? The Yankees hit just .227 and ranked 26th in runs per game without Judge in the lineup this season.

– The Rockies are the worst team in baseball once again. They became just the fifth MLB franchise to lose at least 100 games in four consecutive seasons, last done by the expansion New York Mets (1962-65). They looked pathetic in their final homestand getting trounced by the Diamondbacks.

They will go down in history as the first team to post the highest ERA in five consecutive seasons while also losing at least 100 games in four consecutive years.

– Congratulations to Pete Alonso, who became the first player in MLB history to hit 40 or more home runs in his first season with a team in the National League and the American League, and with 43 homers and 113 RBIs this season, could become the first player ever to lead both leagues in RBI.

– The Yankees are worth at least $12 billion after reaching a deal to sell 16% of the team for $2.6 billion to Apollo Sports Capital (ASC) last month.

– The San Francisco Giants' embarrassing season comes to a close by becoming the first team in four years to go an entire season without a four-game winning streak.

– In 2024 season, the Mariners' rotation produced an MLB-leading 92 quality starts. This year, just 66, with a 4.64 ERA the second half.

– Congratulations AL West, you just produced the worst division in history, with the division champion being the first not to have a winning record.

– Tropicana Field is a house of horrors to visiting teams with the Rays going 55-26 at home this season, and will have home-field advantage throughout the AL postseason.

– What's the difference between hosting a wild-card series and playing on the road?

The home team receives about $3 million in revenue from hosting the first round while the visiting team spends about $1 million with traveling costs.

– The Blue Jays' offensive ineptitude was alarming this year, scoring the fewest runs in MLB with only rookie Kazuma Okamoto hitting more than 15 home runs this season, and only two players with more than 10.

– Chris Sale produced the fifth-lowest ERA (2.16) at the age of 37 or older in MLB history, trailing only: Justin Verlander (1.75 in 2022), Roger Clemens (1.87 in 2005), Dazzy Vance (2.08 in 1928) and Spud Chandler (2.10 in 1946).

– The Mets not only lost plenty on the field this season, but also at the box office.

The Mets' attendance was down 14.8% from last season, averaging 33,901 fans a game, going from fifth in attendance to 12th, with their only sellout on opening day.

– The Yankees are expected to start Max Fried in Game 1 and Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler in Game 2 of the wild-card series against the Red Sox, which still allows Schlittler to pitch Games 2 and 5 in a potential ALDS.

– The San Diego Padres were 50-53 on July 23, with only the 11th-best record in the National League.

Now, they are in the postseason, going on a 15-3 run since Sept. 5, and will likely host the NL Wild Card series.

– Outfielder Austin Hays is in his fourth consecutive postseason with four different teams: Baltimore (2023), Philadelphia (2024), Cincinnati (2025), San Diego (2026).

– Diamondbacks starter Corbin Burnes, who signed a six-year, $210 million contract two years ago, will not opt out of the remaining four years and $140 million on his deal after ending his season on the injured list. He pitched just 10.1 innings in three starts this season recovering from Tommy John surgery, yielding a 7.84 ERA.

– Considering that first baseman Ty France may be the Padres' MVP this season, it wouldn't surprise a soul if the Padres' ownership gives him his $200,000 bonus for reaching 500 plate appearances, even if he's going to fall just shy of the incentive.

– The Padres may have had a losing record against the other NL postseason teams, but no one in baseball had a better record (59-28) against teams with losing records.

– Casey Mize's free-agent value has severely tumbled with his struggles since joining the Padres at the trade deadline, yielding a 7.46 ERA in 10 starts.

Millions of people along the East Coast are bracing for a powerful nor'easter that is expected to bring heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding from the Carolinas to Maine, forecasters say.

The storm, which formed off the mid-Atlantic coast, is expected to stall as it approaches the Northeast and New England, according to the National Weather Service, increasing the likelihood of flooding and beach erosion in parts of New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts.

The Jersey Shore, Long Island and Cape Cod could see up to 3 feet of inundation, especially during high tides.

"This storm may be remembered for its destructive coastal flooding and severe beach erosion, especially along eastern Long Island and the Massachusetts coast," AccuWeather Chief Meteorologist Jon Porter said.

The system has already caused coastal flooding in parts of North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland and Delaware. A stretch of highway on North Carolina's Outer Banks was closed due to "severe overwash" on the roadway.

"We expect similar conditions to continue over the next few high tide cycles until the storm passes," North Carolina's Department of Transportation said on Facebook. "There is currently no timeline on reopening the highway."

Curious what's coming next where you live? Check the new Yahoo Weather app.

Wind gusts of up to 55 mph are expected across the region, which could lead to widespread power outages.

"Given long-duration wind and rain under full foliage, damaging winds will blow down numerous tree limbs, scattered trees and power lines," the National Weather Service's New York office warned.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani issued a travel advisory, encouraging residents to allow extra time and avoid low-lying coastal roads during high tide.

"If you live in a basement apartment, know your way out and be prepared to move to a higher floor if conditions become dangerous," the mayor said in a post on X.

Up to 5 inches of rain is possible in some areas, including eastern Long Island, Rhode Island and Massachusetts.

In anticipation of travel delays, three major airlines — American, United and JetBlue — waived fees for flight changes for travelers from New York City to Boston Friday through Sunday.

The storm has already prompted the organizers of Oceans Calling in Ocean City, Md., to cancel the three-day music festival.

"Tides, floods, and high winds have prevented us from safely continuing the build of Oceans Calling," the festival said in a statement. "Following the advice of the National Weather Service and in cooperation with local public officials, we must make the difficult decision to cancel Oceans Calling 2026."

The Global Citizen Festival, scheduled for Saturday in Central Park, was also canceled.

All Things Go NYC, a three-day music festival set for Forest Hills Stadium in Queens, N.Y., was scrapped by its organizers. But All Things Go D.C., at Merriweather Post Pavilion in Columbia, Md., remains scheduled for this weekend.

The New York Yankees moved Saturday's home game against the Baltimore Orioles up a day due to the impending nor'easter. The clubs are now scheduled to play a single-admission doubleheader on Friday. The Boston Red Sox moved Sunday's home game against the Chicago Cubs to Friday, when the teams will play a doubleheader.

Ed Sheeran's controversial tour canceled two shows that had been scheduled for Gillette Stadium in Foxboro, Mass., due to the forecast.

"Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium," the tour's promoter, Messina Touring, said in a statement posted to Instagram. "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority."

title: White Sox SS Colson Montgomery ties MLB single-season strikeout record that has stood for 17 years
description: Montgomery notched his 223rd strikeout of the season on Thursday, tying a record set in 2009 by Mark Reynolds.
fullText:
On Thursday, as the Chicago White Sox clinched their first playoff berth in five seasons, their shortstop made a little bit of history with one of MLB's least desired records.

With one strikeout in the White Sox's 9-1 win over the Kansas City Royals, shortstop Colson Montgomery tied MLB's record for the most strikeouts in a single season, surpassing a record that had stood for 17 years. Montgomery now has 223 strikeouts on the season, with three games remaining before Chicago heads to the postseason.

Montgomery struck out in the third inning of Thursday's game, with reliever Anthony Gose dispatching him during his third at-bat after the White Sox got off to a hot start. The 24-year-old shortstop went 0-4 on the day, flying out three times in addition to his historic strikeout.

Luisangel Acuña pinch hit for Montgomery in his final at-bat in the ninth, robbing Montgomery of the chance to pass the record.

The original record, set by former Arizona Diamondbacks infielder Mark Reynolds in 2009, seemed likely to be broken this season thanks to a surge of high-strikeout hitters. Philadelphia Phillies designated hitter Kyle Schwarber is just five strikeouts behind the mark, while Los Angeles Angels shortstop Zach Neto is at 209 strikeouts.

But Montgomery has surged ahead to tie the strikeout title in a sort of come-from-behind win, thanks in part to a late cluster of strikeouts over the last few months. In September alone, Montgomery has had seven games with at least three strikeouts. He has six four-strikeout games stretching across the season.

Even with the high number of strikeouts, Montgomery's hitting hasn't been completely atrocious: Though his batting average (.202) and on-base percentage (.288) have been low, his slugging percentage (.418) and OPS (.701) are technically league average. He has 31 home runs, 112 hits and 87 RBIs.

Multiple players have come close to Reynolds' record over the years, but none have matched the former infielder's mark before this season. Reynolds told The Athletic in July that he used to see the stat as "embarrassing," but now views it as a "badge of honor."

"Now, I'm older. Have perspective. People ask me, 'Do you want someone to break it?' I'm like, 'No. How many big-league records do you have?'" Reynolds said at the time.

In the same interview, Reynolds joked that he might have to hand off the strikeout honor to whoever breaks the record on "SportsCenter." But there's still a nonzero chance that multiple players will pass him, with Schwarber coming around the corner with four games remaining.

For now, though, Montgomery can claim sole ownership of a place in the record books, for better or for worse.

title: No longer defined by 121 losses, White Sox punch ticket to MLB postseason
description: The White Sox completed one of baseball's most stunning turnarounds, clinching a playoff berth after losing 121 games just two seasons ago.
fullText:
This will be remembered as the Chicago White Sox team that made history for all the right reasons.

Two years after losing a Major League Baseball-record 121 games and one year after their third consecutive 100-loss season, the White Sox are going to the playoffs. Their startling resurgence was completed Thursday, Sept. 24 when they defeated the Kansas City Royals 9-1 at Kauffman Stadium to clinch at least an American League wild-card berth.

The South Siders are still playing for a bigger prize. They pulled within a half-game of the Cleveland Guardians in the AL Central with the victory. The Guardians were scheduled to play at Boston later Thursday and close the season with three games against the Royals. The White Sox finish with three games against the Colorado Rockies, who were set to lose their 102nd game Thursday. The White Sox hold the tiebreaker against the Guardians.

Chicago has held first place for 82 games this year and most of the second half, until the Guardians took over Sept. 17. But the White Sox erased no doubt Thursday that they'd nail down a playoff spot.

They scored six runs in the first two innings, thanks to a pair of hits and two RBIs from Miguel Vargas, and after Kyle Teel's fourth-inning homer the rout was on, as right-hander David Sandlin held the Royals to one run over six innings.

Chicago's 82 wins are the most for a team coming off three 100-loss seasons, and second-most after just one 100-loss season. The White Sox also clinched a winning record for the first time since 2021, when they won 93 games and qualified most recently for the playoffs.

Those White Sox were beat in four games by the Houston Astros in the AL division series. These White Sox have a chance to win the division and receive a bye into the ALDS, where they'd face the winner of the AL West champion and No. 3 wild card.

They got here on the strength of several breakout performances and one MVP-caliber level-up from Vargas. Acquired from the Los Angeles Dodgers in a three-team deal that also included the St. Louis Cardinals and sent Tommy Edman to the eventual World Series champions, Vargas put it all together this season, hitting 33 home runs, driving in 92 and posting an .842 OPS. He's also stolen 21 bases and needs just two walks to reach 100.

Rookies Tristan Peters and Sam Antonacci are hitting well above league average, with Peters providing 3.9 WAR thanks to excellent defense in center field. And with Teel returning from injuries, the return haul in the trade of Garrett Crochet to Boston is popping, with second baseman Chase Meidroth posting a .763 OPS and 4.3 WAR and Braden Montgomery part of a platoon in right field.

title: Phillies’ 7-Year Veteran Celebrates Rare MLB Feat With New Team
description: The Philadelphia Phillies have received a remarkable update on a long-time pitcher who left the organization.
fullText:
The Philadelphia Phillies entered the season with one of baseball's deepest starting rotations and the club has managed some turbulence and changes to retain that strength amid another playoff push.

With Cristopher Sanchez setting a franchise record earlier this season, Zack Wheeler fighting through a return from offseason surgery and Aaron Nola and Andrew Painter finding their strides, Philadelphia's rotation depth has remained a significant part of its postseason plans.

Under president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski, starting pitching has long been the Phillies' calling card. And that included the career start of a player who has now earned a notable career accomplishment with his new team.

Former Mets Backstop Suddenly Ends Career Just 8 Days Before Season Finale

Zach Eflin, who spent the first seven seasons of his career with the Phillies before moving on to the Tampa Bay Rays and then the Baltimore Orioles, has officially reached 10 years of MLB service time.

The Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA) marked the occasion with an announcement on social media.

The milestone carries particular significance because reaching a decade of service requires much more than simply having major league talent. Players must remain healthy and productive enough to spend years in the majors while navigating injuries, roster decisions and the natural turnover of professional baseball.

When it comes to Eflin, many Phillies fans will take the moment to remember his dependability and contributions across many years in Philadelphia.

"Throughout history, fewer than 10% of Players have possessed the combination of talent, health, resilience, perseverance and good fortune to achieve the feat," MLBPA noted in the announcement. "Eflin was selected by San Diego in the first round of the 2012 draft and debuted with the Phillies four years later. Eflin spent his first seven seasons in Philadelphia before stints in Tampa Bay and Baltimore. The Florida native has pitched in over 200 games and accumulated more than 900 strikeouts."

Eflin's Philadelphia tenure included several different stages of his development, including the start of what became a standout career in the majors.

Eflin's biggest transformation came after he moved away from an approach centered on overpowering hitters and instead leaned more heavily on his sinker and curveball, thanks in large part to the Phillies' development system. That adjustment helped him become a more effective major league starter, including a 2020 season in which he posted a 3.97 ERA and 10.9 strikeouts per nine innings.

Injuries interrupted his time with Philadelphia, including season-ending knee surgery in 2021. But he later became an important part of the Phillies' 2022 postseason bullpen, posting a 3.38 ERA across 10 and two-thirds playoff innings.

After the 2022 season, Eflin left Philadelphia and signed a three-year, $40 million contract with the Rays. Now, more than a decade after being drafted, the former Phillies pitcher has reached one of baseball's most exclusive career milestones.

title: How the Cubs Playoff Rotation is Shaping Up
description: With the MLB postseason race shaping up, the Chicago Cubs' playoff rotation is becoming clearer. They have occasionally had a rough time with their pitching staff this season, and it has been hard to know who they can trust. However, they are heading for a best-of-three series in the Wild Card round. This means that …
fullText:
With the MLB postseason race shaping up, the Chicago Cubs' playoff rotation is becoming clearer. They have occasionally had a rough time with their pitching staff this season, and it has been hard to know who they can trust. However, they are heading for a best-of-three series in the Wild Card round. This means that they need to start figuring out which three starters make the cut.

Clay Holmes feels safely locked into being one of the three pitchers in the Cubs playoff rotation. Chicago made a massive trade to acquire Holmes at the deadline. Since he returned from injury, it has been worth the cost. He is one of the key players for the Cubs' run in October.

Although his 4.26 ERA is not amazing, it does not tell the full story. He had a strong stretch before struggling in the past three starts, allowing 16 earned runs. This makes it a little concerning, but before that he was rock solid and one of the team's best starters. In four starts before, he allowed only one run. His ability to force ground balls fits in perfectly with the Cubs' elite defense.

Now, the Cubs could play it safe with Holmes and limit his usage over the final week of the regular season. He would be set for one final start, where it may help to play him to get things right. It may be too long of a gap between games, so it would be a surprise if he does not at least pitch a few innings in a game. Before his struggles, it looked like he would be a possible game one starter. Even if he does not get that role, it feels highly unlikely that he does not get a postseason start.

One of the other big trade deadline additions was Kevin Gausman. He is the most experienced pitcher for Chicago, appearing in plenty of postseason games. Since coming to the team, he has given the team good length. Additionally, Chicago has won a majority of his starts.

Heading into his September 23rd start against the Marlins, he has a rough 5.04 ERA with the Cubs. However, like Holmes, that has been inflated by rough games. Gausman is still 4-2 in 44 2/3 innings pitched. His ability to go deep into games is needed with Chicago's rough bullpen. There is a possibility that he is not in the Cubs playoff rotation for the wild card round. Although his experience and durability make it hard not to rely on him.

The third spot is where it gets tricky. Technically, this spot is not guaranteed. If either team wins both of the first two games, the series wouldn't need a third starter. However, if Chicago advanced, the Cubs playoff rotation would be expanded. With this in mind, Matthew Boyd would likely be in the Cubs playoff rotation for the first round.

Boyd has been a reliable option for Chicago this year when he has stayed healthy. He is 9-5 with a 4.06 ERA. The veteran lefty also has plenty of experience at Wrigley Field. If Chicago secures the top Wild Card spot, this would be an advantage. He could very well start either of the first two games as well. The only pitcher possibly above him in the order is Holmes. Boyd and Gausman could come down to which team they face and how they fare against the veteran pitchers.

Shota Imanaga and David Peterson are also hanging around for a possible start. Imanaga is hard to trust with his home run issue, but has seemed to stabilize himself. Peterson is stringing together good starts, and he could very well start in the playoffs. All of the pitchers have question marks around them, but these two may have fewer answers.

When looking at the Cubs playoff rotation, there are multiple ways Chicago can go. All of the starters have shown flashes, but also had very rough games. They still have a week to go, and the decision could be impacted by their opponent. Holmes, Gausman, and Boyd have seemed to separate themselves a bit. Regardless of who gets which game, they will need to set the tone for the series, as it is nearly impossible to trust the bullpen.
