title: One fatal flaw on each MLB contender that could derail long playoff run
description: From the Rays' bottom of the order to the Dodgers' shaky bullpen, every playoff contender is carrying one weakness that could end its October early.
fullText:
Entering the last week of the Major League Baseball season, 13 teams are still alive for October, and not one of them would be considered a totally complete team.

The Milwaukee Brewers have the best record in baseball but just one starter behind its ace it can actually trust. The Tampa Bay Rays are on the verge of clinching the top seed in the American League but have a lineup that goes cold at the bottom of the order almost every night. And a few teams, like the New York Yankees, are staring down injuries that can make or break their October.

Last season proved how a fatal flaw can come back and bite a team in October.

The Brewers had the best record in baseball in 2025 then scored one run a game and hit .128 in a four-game National League Championship Series sweep by the Dodgers. It was the lowest batting average in a postseason series of at least three games in MLB history. Their power outage was not a fluke. Milwaukee finished the year in the bottom third of the majors in home runs, covering for it all season with contact and speed. The flaw was there, buried under 97 wins, and it was exploited once the bright lights came on.

Here's the one fatal flaw that could end each contender's season:

MLB POSTSEASON FIELD: Who has clinched berths and who's on the verge?

The Rays have the best record in the American League (95-60, through Sept. 20) and need only a win or a New Yankees loss to clinch the AL East and home field advantage through the ALCS. Their flaw is buried at the bottom of the order. The seventh, eighth and ninth spots in the lineup rank 24th in the majors in OPS. Taylor Walls is hitting .219 with a .609 OPS in 52 games. Jorge Mateo has a .397 OPS in 23 games since Tampa Bay acquired him. The Rays have been burned by this flaw before. In 2023,the bottom of their lineup went 3-for-17 with no runs scored in a two-game sweep by Texas in the Wild Card Series, part of a 33-inning postseason scoreless streak.

The Yankees lead the majors with a 3.08 bullpen ERA, but Aaron Boone trusts exactly three relievers with a game on the line: closer David Bednar and setup men Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn. Every reinforcement behind them has left doubt in Boone's mind. New York traded a struggling Camilo Doval away at the deadline instead of adding to the pen, then lost Fernando Cruz to a partial UCL tear in late August. Ryan Weathers, the next man up, hasn't pitched since Aug. 23. Blackburn and Headrick had already thrown 79 and 73 innings heading into Sunday's game, more than typical setup men carry into a pennant race, let alone October. History carries a warning for the Yankees here. Cleveland's bullpen led the majors in the second half of 2016, but manager Terry Francona rode just two trusted arms hard, Andrew Miller and Cody Allen, through October. Both were spent by Game 7, and Cleveland ended up blowing a 3-1 World Series lead. One bad week from the bullpen and the Yankees are heading to the golf course instead of the World Series.

Boston clinched a playoff berth Sunday, Sept. 20 depite losing and hold the second AL wild card at 84-72, but its bullpen depth beyond three arms is the real question. Justin Slaten is done for the season, a degenerative elbow injury discovered too late to fix with anything but rest. Tyron Guerrero has been out since Sept. 1 with shoulder inflammation. Closer Aroldis Chapman, 34 saves and a 1.95 ERA, is nursing lat tightness, which already forced Garrett Whitlock, an ERA near 1.80 himself, into save situations he's never handled before. Boston gave up infield prospect Marcelo Mayer in August just to get reliever Erik Miller. That's how thin the bullpen was even before the injuries hit.

A thin bullpen is a real weakness in October, as the Orioles showed in 2023. Felix Bautista suffered a season-ending elbow injury just weeks before the playoffs and Baltimore went on to be swept in the American League Division Series.

The White Sox lost their lead in the AL Central, and part of the reason is a red flag for the playoffs. If they get in, the worry is that their rotation can't get through a lineup twice. Sean Burke went six innings against Detroit on Sept. 19, the first White Sox starter to complete six innings since Aug. 21. That's nearly a month of bullpen games in disguise. Trade deadline pickup Luis Castillo got pulled from the rotation entirely and moved to relief after his outings collapsed. His replacement, rookie David Sandlin, has an ERA near 7. Anthony Kay has been yanked early in four straight starts. Sean Newcomb, who carried the bullpen for months, has allowed runs in five of his last six outings. Chicago fell out of first place in the AL Central for the first time since early July, and it wasn't the offense that let go.

Cleveland's bullpen has no safety net. Closer Cade Smith has carried the group all year, but Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, the two relievers who were supposed to set up in front of him, haven't thrown a competitive pitch all season. Both are on unpaid leave while awaiting a federal trial on pitch-rigging charges – now pushed to November – which puts them out for the postseason, too. The relievers brought in to cover that gap keep breaking down. Colin Holderman aggravated a wrist injury on a rehab outing Sept. 17. Shawn Armstrong, out since July 25 with a calf strain, isn't eligible to be back until Sept. 23. Cleveland is leaning on arms with no October track record to hold leads under the most pressure of the year

Houston's bridge to Josh Hader has collapsed. The Astros trail Texas by one game in the AL West with six left, and the two setup relievers who were supposed to get games to him are both hurt. Steven Okert, their best setup arm, hasn't pitched since Sept. 1 with a hamstring strain and won't be back before the postseason ... if there is one. Enyel De Los Santos joined him on the injured list Sept. 19. That leaves Bennett Sousa, who has a 5.27 ERA and control problems, and Bryan Abreu, who blew a save the same day in a loss that knocked Houston out of a playoff spot. That's two hurt setup arms and a shaky one left standing. That is not a formula for October.

The Rangers lead the AL West by one game over Houston, but the bullpen behind Jacob Latz wasn't built for this. Texas lost two relievers for the season – Carter Baumler and Jalen Beeks – and designated veteran Chris Martin for assignment in August after a 7.00 ERA. That left Latz, a converted starter, as closer by default. He converted nine consecutive saves before blowing one against Boston on Sept. 18. Days later, Skip Schumaker had nobody left in the pen and had to use starter Nathan Eovaldi for relief innings, then Jordan Montgomery for more two days after that.

A starter coming out of the bullpen isn't that crazy in the playoffs, but a bullpen held together by starters filling in is a screaming warning siren.

Spencer Schwellenbach and Hurston Waldrep both had season-ending elbow surgery in late August – Schwellenbach's second in under a year. Bryce Elder had knee surgery in September. Reynaldo López has been on and off the injured list twice, most recently Sept. 15. That is four rotation arms gone and leaves Chris Sale, 14-9 with a 2.18 ERA, and Tyler Mahle, sharp since he arrived from San Francisco, as the only settled postseason starters Atlanta has. The Braves have tried this before. In 2013 they lost Tim Hudson and Brandon Beachy to injuries, went into October with only Kris Medlen and Mike Minor as trusted starters and rode 37-year-old Freddy Garcia to a Game 4 exit in a 3-1 NLDS loss.

The Phillies traded for Jhoan Duran for just this time of year, and he hasn't disappointed. The problem for Philadelphia is getting to him. Orion Kerkering, their setup man for most of the year, got optioned to Triple-A on Sept. 19 after an ERA above 8.00 since the All-Star break. Jonathan Bowlan, who took over the eighth inning, is playing through a groin strain. What's left is rookie Alex McFarlane and September call-up Max Lazar in the highest-leverage innings of the year. Philadelphia holds the last NL wild card spot at 86-70, a game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres, with no margin for what comes next.

Milwaukee may have the best record in baseball – 98-58 through Sunday – but they run out of starters really fast. Jacob Misiorowski is a bona fide ace and the likely NL Cy Young winner, and Logan Henderson has quietly gone 10-3 with an ERA near 2.50 behind him. After that, it's question marks. The Brewers traded Freddy Peralta in January then lost Brandon Woodruff and Quinn Priester to season-ending surgery. Kyle Harrison was supposed to be the answer behind Misiorowski. He had a 2.57 ERA before the All-Star break. Since then, it's over 7.00, including four earned runs in one and two-thirds innings against Pittsburgh on Sept. 17. Deadline pickup Dustin May is an unproven fourth option with little margin for error. The best record in baseball still needs pitching to win a series.

The Cubs will take the best offense in baseball into October – 835 runs scored through Sept. 20, the most in the majors – and pair it with the pitching staff most likely to give a game away. Chicago's pitchers have allowed 227 home runs, also a league high. Cade Horton needed Tommy John surgery in April and won't pitch again this year. Ben Brown was shut down for good in September with a neck injury. Justin Steele hasn't started a big league game since April 2025. Deadline addition Kevin Gausman has a 5.04 ERA in eight starts as a Cub. Clay Holmes had a 1.55 ERA in his first five Cubs starts then allowed eight earned runs in 4⅓ innings against Miami on Sept. 6, leaving Craig Counsell still deciding whether he trusts him in October. It's happened to a loaded lineup before. The Dodgers scored 906 runs in 2023 – the second most in baseball that season – then watched Lance Lynn set a playoff record allowing four home runs in one inning as Arizona swept them out of the NLDS. Even the best offense in baseball can't outscore its own pitchers giving up home runs like this.

The Dodgers' bullpen problem is bigger than one bad closer. Edwin Diaz posted an 11.85 ERA before a neck injury, then came back Sept. 18 after a rehab stint so bad he retired two of eight batters in one outing. Dave Roberts didn't give him the ninth inning back. His replacement, Tanner Scott, isn't clean either. He blew a save against Miami on Sept. 13, his fourth in 26 chances. Setup man Edgardo Henriquez, who has a 2.85 ERA, went down with a back strain Sept. 14 and won't pitch again this season. A bullpen implosion has cost the Dodgers before. The 106-win 2019 team kept turning to Joe Kelly until he finally served up a series-ending grand slam. Los Angeles clinched its fifth consecutive NL West title with a bullpen nobody trusts yet.

Luis Rengifo was hitting .291 with a .784 OPS when he tore his ACL on Aug. 29. He is done for the year, and so is the San Diego bench really. Gavin Sheets has been out with a foot injury since late August. Ramón Laureano's absence has stretched deep into September. The Padres are tied with the Cubs and one game ahead of the Phillies for wild card positioning but sitting on the wrong side of the tiebreakers to both teams. They are filling in with September call-ups instead of players they built the roster around, and there isn't much season left to figure out if that holds up. The 2012 Yankees tried that when they lost Derek Jeter to a broken ankle in the ALCS opener; they got nothing much from the bench options and were swept by Detroit hitting .157 as a team.

fullText:
The Milwaukee Brewers set a franchise record last year by going 97-65. Not only did they finish with the best record in baseball, but they also had more wins than any other team in the history of the organization.

Now, a year later, they are even better.

With their 3-0 win over the Baltimore Orioles on Sunday night, Milwaukee improved to 98-58 on the season. Obviously, this breaks their franchise record from last season, and also marks the first time in franchise history that they are 40 games over .500.

Oh, and Jackson Chourio made history, too.

Heading into the game, Chourio had 24 home runs and 19 stolen bases on the season. He swiped two bags in the 3-0 victory, giving him his third consecutive 20-20 season to start his Major League career.

This milestone is notable for two reasons. First, he joins Julio Rodriguez and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only three players in baseball history to start their careers with three straight 20-20 seasons.

But what is even more impressive is that Chourio, who is still just 22 years old, is the first player in history to have three consecutive 20-20 seasons before the age of 23:

Jackson Chourio swipes his 20th bag of the season

He is the first player with 3 seasons of 20+ stolen bases and 20+ home runs before turning 23 years old! pic.twitter.com/3PwbpjxM3a

— MLB (@MLB) September 21, 2026

What makes the achievement all the more impressive this year is the fact that Chourio missed the first month of the season with a fracture in his left hand. Had he been healthy in March/April, he likely would have accomplished this milestone weeks ago, and perhaps would have a 30-30 season by now.

For the 2026 season, the Brewers' star left-fielder is hitting .285/.344/.481 with 24 home runs, 70 RBI, and 21 stolen bases.

Oh, and he leads all MLB left fielders in defensive runs saved, making him a serious candidate for a Gold Glove award.

It's no secret that the 2026 campaign has been a roller coaster for Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes. His play has been rather inconsistent, as he's been nowhere near his Cy Young-caliber self all year. While his play has been alarming, manager Don Kelly is not yet ready to hit the panic button.

During a guest appearance on MLB Radio, Kelly praised the 24-year-old right-hander for at least maintaining his work ethic throughout the season. After two incredible years to begin his career, Kelly is impressed with Skenes' approach during what's been considered a down year for the superstar pitcher.

"Paul set the bar so high in his first two years, having a sub-2.00 ERA, winning the Cy Young, and Rookie of the Year," Kelly said. "I think the thing with Paul is the work ethic, the commitment to excellence, how he's continued to push himself, even through the first two years, and certainly this year, in trying to continue to grind to get better. Every day, Pinstripe Alley offers updates on what the Yankees' top American League opponents are up to through the Rivalry Roundup. Top Position Player: Yordan Alvarez (5.8 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Peter Lambert (2.4 fWAR)

Much like a panicked squashed cockroach in a muggy South Texas roadside motel, the Astros currently find themselves right at .500 but somehow leading the division. What I mean is they're barely alive, but still living their dream in a division that is a trashcan.

The rest of the way the Astros start with four games at home versus lowly Kansas City and then welcome the NL East leading Braves to Space City for a three game set. Houston then finishes the year with two games in Seattle before finishing the season with a four-game set with the Athletics.

Houston might very well walk away from what should be a disappointing season in terms of record with a division crown, triple-crown winner, and possible MVP. Why the baseball Gods feel inclined to continue to bless this abomination of a ball club is beyond me.

Top Position Player: Ezequiel Durán (4.7 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Jacob deGrom (4.1 fWAR)

The other Texas team came into the month with a chance to run down their instate foes but have not done anything to make it easier on themselves after starting September 5-6. The odds makers currently have the Rangers' playoffs chances around 30 percent. And it might just be recency bias, but the Rangers seem like the hottest team out west with their current two-game win streak.

The Rangers' next game kicks off a nine game homestand. The Red Sox are the first team to come to town, followed by the Blue Jays, and then the Mets crash the party. All three series are three games apiece. The Rangers then close the season in Minnesota with another three game set against the Twins.

Not having a single game left against the AL West hurts the Rangers chances to run down the Astros. Another Texas-sized problem for the Rangers is the fact their lone star neighbors hold the tiebreaker so they are really an additional game back in the standings. With 12 games left to go will the Rangers be able to free the world from having to watch the Astros in the playoffs?

Top Position Player: Randy Arozarena (4.3 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Bryan Woo (3.7 fWAR)

While I would say the Tigers have to hold the torch for the most disappointing team in 2026, the Mariners might be the challenger for that top spot. Seattle's sky high expectations are all but sleepless at this point, unless they find some magic and get some help.

In order to reach the .500 mark, that might be all that is needed to win the west, the Mariners would need to be near perfect. They honestly have the schedule to pull it off, but it is hard to sweep teams. Starting today the Mariners are in LA for three games against the Angels, then shoot over to Denver to face the punching bag of a club in the Rockies for three games. Seattle returns home for the final six, with two against the Astros, before getting the Angels for the last four games of the season.

The Mariners have already clinched the tiebreaker versus the Astros on the season. It is very unlikely, but having the tiebreaker is huge and if the Astros slip the Mariners very well could be the team that squeaks their way into the division crown.

Top Position Player: Nick Kurtz (2.6 fWAR)
Top Pitchers: J.T. Ginn (1.7 fWAR)

The team formerly from Oakland always comes into the season looking at true two outcomes. They either surprise and find themselves at the top of the division with players to be traded later, or they bottom out like they did this season. The Athletics have one more year before relocating to Vegas.

On a Yankees note, the Athletics are our second favorite team this week as they face the Rays starting on Tuesday for a three game set in the Trop. It might be a bad bet, but maybe the Athletics will be able to channel ghosts of decades past and take one or two games before leaving Florida.

Top Position Players: Mike Trout and Zach Neto (3.3 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Reid Detmers (4.4 fWAR)

The Angels might finally, ironically, have a light at the end of the tunnel as they will be under new ownership after the 2026 season. Change cannot come fast enough for the team battling the Rockies for the league's worst record.

title: Tampa Bay Rays first to clinch MLB playoff berth on Junior Caminero walk-off homer
description: The Tampa Bay Rays are the first team to lock up a spot in the 2026 MLB playoffs. They did it in dramatic fashion.
fullText:
The Tampa Bay Rays became the first major league club to clinch a 2026 playoff berth - and they did so in walk-off fashion thanks to their superstar third baseman.

Junior Caminero hit his 40th home run of the season, a two-run shot off Houston Astros reliever Bryan Abreu, and the Rays punched their postseason ticket in the giddiest fashion possible, beating the Astros 3-1 Friday, Sept. 11 at Tropicana Field.

The Rays (88-59) return to the postseason for the first time since 2023, when they won 99 games but were eliminated by the eventual champion Texas Rangers in the wild-card round.

This season, their sights are set much higher.

The Rays retain a three-game lead over the New York Yankees in the American League East, and the division champion is nearly assured the top seed in the AL and a first-round bye. Tampa Bay entered Friday with an 81% chance to win the divison, according to FanGraphs.

Jonathan Aranda nearly ended it a batter earlier, when his shot to right center field hit just below the yellow line on the outfield fence. He settled for a one-out double. Caminero then leaned back and blasted an Abreu first-pitch fastball 417 feet over the wall in left, his AL-leading 40th of the season.

JUNIOR CAMINERO WALKS IT OFF@RAYSBASEBALL HEADS TO THE POSTSEASON! pic.twitter.com/tkDpYi0OEe

Caminero pounded his chest twice, exhorted his teammates in the Rays dugout and commenced a joyous trip around the bases as Tropicana Field roared.

That culminated a crisp ballgame in which starter Drew Rasmussen pitched seven innings of one-run ball. Closer Bryan Baker pitched a scoreless ninth to earn the win.

Tampa Bay has the AL's best record for a reason, a club with one legitimate superstar in third baseman Caminero and a slew of well-fitting parts. The Rays lineup is a daunting combination of power and speed, with Caminero's AL-leading 40 home runs tucked in the lineup around slugger Yandy Díaz (22 homers, .835 OPS) and first baseman Aranda (19 homers, .359 OBP). Speedy Chandler Simpson ranks second in the AL with a .306 average and the club makes contact better than any team in the majors.

Meanwhile, right-handers Nick Martinez and Rasmussen have combined for a 28-5 record and ERAs of 2.92 and 2.81, respectively.

Tampa Bay has two games remaining with the Astros before hosting the Athletics for three games. And then the road gets tougher to finish the season.

The Rays host third-place Boston for three games before a challenging seven-game road trip, beginning with four games at Yankee Stadium Sept. 22-24 that should go a long way toward determining the division title. Tampa Bay finishes the regular season with three games at NL wild-card hopeful Philadelphia.

If the Rays hold on and win the division, they will play host to Game 1 of the five-game AL Division Series on Saturday, Oct. 3.

Isaac Paredes worked some two out magic launching a 2-run blast, his 19th of the year, which brought home Yordan Alvarez. Moments earlier, Alvarez drove in Cam Smith on a double to deep right center. Altuve's historic double preceded a Yainer Diaz singlethat drove him in, making it 4-0.

Trea Turner sent one to the seats getting one of those runs back in the fifth. Then in the sixth, the wheels officially came off.

Hunter Brown, who was making his 17th start of the year, went five innings. He'd allow 4 runs on 7 hits while striking out 7. Enter Bryan King. Bryan De La Cruz drew a bases loaded walk which gave Philly the lead, and they'd never relinquish it. At one point, AJ threw a sequence of six straight balls. Tatsuya Imai started the bottom half of the seventh issuing back-to-back walks but settled down. Once again in the 8th, Imai allowed multiple base runners to reach but got out unscathed.

The Astros and Phillies would combine for 24 hits on the night.

description: Cam Schlittler continues to be a revelation.

New York Yankees starting pitcher Cam Schlittler has accomplished something rarely seen on an MLB mound.

He joins Randy Johnson as the only modern-era pitcher to produce a streak of this length while striking out more batters than hits allowed on the road.

Aug 21, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Cam Schlittler (31) pitches against the Toronto Blue Jays during the first inning at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Schlittler delivered another dominant performance in the Yankees' 6-3 victory over the Los Angeles Angels last night. The right-hander struck out nine batters while allowing just two hits across eight innings, continuing what has become an extraordinary run away from New York.

With his latest outing, Schlittler has now recorded more strikeouts than hits allowed in each of his last 21 road starts. The streak dates back to August 2, 2025, and during that span, the Yankees sophomore has struck out 157 batters while surrendering only 70 hits.

That puts Schlittler in rare company. The only other pitcher in the modern era to achieve a streak of at least this length was Johnson, who accomplished the feat across 23 games with the Arizona Diamondbacks from 1999 to 2000.

His consistency has also played a major role in keeping the Yankees firmly in the American League playoff picture. New York currently holds the first Wild Card spot with an 80-60 record and a 9.5-game cushion.

The Yankees will now turn their attention toward a weekend series in San Diego against the Padres. With Schlittler continuing to pitch at an elite level, New York has another major weapon as it looks to secure its postseason position.

If his historic road dominance continues, Schlittler could finish the season not only as one of the Yankees' most important players, but also as one of the American League's premier starting pitchers.

title: Who Will Win the Worst Division Battle in MLB History?
description: The 2026 season of Major League Baseball and its oddities will be looked back on for years to come. There’s an extraordinary power difference between leagues. There could potentially be the first sub-.500 playoff team ever. There’s also a blatantly terrible, yet potentially historic, division race among everything else the 2026 season has challenged.
fullText:
The 2026 season of Major League Baseball and its oddities will be looked back on for years to come.

There's an extraordinary power difference between leagues. There could potentially be the first sub-.500 playoff team ever. There's also a blatantly terrible, yet potentially historic, division race among everything else the 2026 season has challenged.

The American League West can make baseball history in September. The worst division winner ever belongs to the 2005 San Diego Padres. That Bruce Bochy-led club finished 82-80, good enough to take the National League West by five games.

Entering the final month of the MLB season, the Houston Astros lead the AL West with a fragile 70-68 record. They're two full games up on the second-place team, and up five from third-place. That said, given how the wild West has fared, those standings and positions could change or get worse in the blink of an eye.

This division held three .500 teams from the previous season, including one that nearly won the American League. The Seattle Mariners entered as the clear favorite, coming off an ALCS appearance and were one of the premier clubs coming into 2026.

Houston has won the West seven times in the last decade, but is transitioning outside of their dynastic era. However, they're not the most recent team with a World Series in the division. The Texas Rangers bought in and won their only title in franchise history in 2023, but have failed to replicate the magic since. The Astros and Rangers came into the season as potential sleeper teams, but without real postseason aspirations.

The Los Angeles Angels and Athletics were both projected in the basement of the division, stuck in rebuilds. With all of these ambitions set to play out in the Mariners' shadow, nothing has gone as expected.

All five teams have been in first at some point this season. In fact, Seattle has spent some of the least amount of time in first among their division counterparts.

Seattle started slow, giving the Rangers and Athletics space to battle through the first month. Surprisingly enough, the A's either led or were tied for first for 45 straight days starting April 11.

After a 9-1 victory on May 27, the Mariners properly took first and held it. For well over a month, Seattle teetered their record around .500 while keeping the lead. Their governance lasted until the Rangers rode a win streak into July and captured first place for the All-Star break.

The Astros didn't sit idly by for long, taking over the Rangers' spot on July 31. They've led since, but are in no position to begin thinking about October.

This AL West battle between three mediocre teams could be the most exciting story to follow as the season concludes. It's down to the Astros, Rangers and Mariners, who as of Aug. 30 have a combined winning percentage of 48%.

Similar to how the West started with the Mariners, it will end with the Mariners. Over the 24 total games Seattle plays in September, 19 of them are intradivisional. That includes seven games each against the A's and Angels, and one series apiece with the Rangers and Astros.

Oppositely, both Texas and Houston have played the majority of their division series. After a treacherous final month, the Astros embark on a six-game road trip to complete the season. They'll play two games in Seattle and then four in Sacramento against the Athletics.

Texas finishes a home series against the A's to open the month, then visits the Mariners a week later. The Rangers and Astros do not meet in September.

This disordered schedule actually sets up a world where everything could be decided on the final day. On Sept. 27, the Astros play the A's while the Mariners play the Angels. The Rangers travel North and finish their season against the Minnesota Twins, who are also competing for the Wild Card.

All three games would take place at the same time, potentially while delivering baseball history.

Although the Astros have been atop the table since July, the Rangers and Mariners still have a suitable chance.

The biggest obstacle in the Astros' way is not their division opponents, but their schedule itself. Houston plays five clubs that currently hold a playoff spot through the final month. With 24 games remaining, that gives them the 9th hardest strength of schedule. That's by far the most difficult of any team in the AL West.

In the same breath, the Rangers stare down three playoff teams. However, they don't necessarily need to focus on winning the division. As of Aug. 30, they sit two games back from the final Wild Card spot in the American League. There has never been a team outside the extended 2020 playoff format to reach October with a losing record. Texas could become the first if they can't catch the Astros but remain in the race. Or, hell, they could just win the division under .500 and make the postseason regardless.

Do you know which team isn't affected by a hard remaining strength of schedule? The Seattle Mariners. As a matter of fact, they have the easiest in all of baseball. They also have the clear-cut best intradivision record in the AL West. They've gone 20-13 thus far, which suits their division-heavy schedule through September well.

FanGraphs gives Houston a 67% chance to win its eighth division title in the last 10 years. Texas trails with 19%, and Seattle follows with 12%. The trio is projected to finish within three games of each other, furthering the potential of multiple make-or-break series in the final week.

It's that time of the year when every pitch matters. There are about 25 games left, and no team from the West has proved their playoff ready. Or ready to win a division, for that matter.

The beauty of baseball lies in how unpredictable things like this can go. Plus, once you make the playoffs, who knows what could happen.

Will the Astros return to the playoffs, where the core of this roster is all too familiar? Can the Rangers really pursue their second-ever World Series? And when – if at all – will the Mariners die?

title: MLB-record $4 billion sale was long time coming for aimless LA Angels
description: Arte Moreno finally sold the Angels in the midst of an MLB-worst postseason drought.
fullText:
The hatred, the criticism, the nastiness, is all over.

They can't get Arte Moreno anymore.

Moreno, who tried to sell the Los Angeles Angels four years ago but changed his mind five months later, remained patient and finally got his price to escape baseball's rat race, just ahead of baseball's anticipated Dec. 1 lockout.

He is selling the franchise for an MLB record $4 billion to sports mogul Stan Kroenke, according to a high-ranking MLB official with knowledge of the agreement. The person spoke on the condition of anonymity because the terms of the deal were not immediately public.

Moreno, 80, who purchased the Angels in 2003, just one year after they won the World Series, becoming baseball's first Latino owner with his wife, Carole, never came close to duplicating the success.

They spent money, brought in some of the biggest stars in the sport with Albert Pujols and Josh Hamilton, and had a franchise player in Mike Trout, earned five division titles in a six-year span, but haven't made the postseason since 2014.

They have the worst team in the American League (53-85), with their postseason drought extending to 12 years, and are on pace to lose 100 games for the first time in franchise history.

Now, after enduring chants of "Sell the Team," with attendance shrinking and Angels' fans turning their backs on the franchise, Moreno decided it was time to get out.

The decision stunned some of his closest friends in the industry, although one associate said he wasn't surprised at all, believing that Moreno already showed signs of losing interest.

Really, we should have all seen this coming. When Moreno fired GM Perry Minasian in June and brought in former St. Louis Cardinals baseball chief John Mozeliak, on the advice of president Molly Jolly, Mozeliak suddenly had more autonomy that existed under the last three Angels GMs.

Mozeliak was able to trade away veteran players like outfielder Jo Adell and starter Jose Soriano for prospects at the deadline, something that Moreno would have prohibited the last two decades. Mozeliak, who brought in nine prospects at the trade deadline, even was permitted to completely restructure his front office this week.

Yet, he refused to allow Minasian to even take serious offers for Shohei Ohtani three years ago at the trade deadline, wanting to re-sign him in the off-season. When Ohtani received his free-agent offers and told Moreno that he'd come back for the same 10-year, $700 million contract that he was being offered by the Los Angeles Dodgers, Toronto Blue Jays and San Francsico Giants – including $680 million in deferrals – Moreno passed without bothering to counter.

Even with the historic amount of deferred money, Moreno told his front office, "It's still $700 million."

So, the Angels received nothing in return for the biggest marketing star in baseball history, let alone the most talented since perhaps Babe Ruth, watching the Dodgers win back-to-back World Series and bring in more than $1 billion in revenue.

While the Dodgers stole the spotlight in Los Angeles, Moreno didn't blink, with their free-agent signings so pedestrian that there was not a single press conference for a free agent in Minasian's 5 ½-year tenure.

The Angels, who have hired five managers since Mike Scioscia's departure after the 2018 season, didn't even allow Minasian to offer any managerial candidate a contract longer than one year. Moreno had planned to hire Pujols, believing that he'd simply accept the $1 million personal services contract he already had with the team as part of his 10-year, $250 million deal. When Pujols asked for more as manager, including the right to hire most of his coaches, he was rejected, and the team turned to front office executive Kurt Suzuki, who accepted a one-year deal.

Moreno now walks away with at least a $3.8 billion profit, and can sit back in his Phoenix estate eating hot dogs and drinking beers watching several ballgames a day, without having to endure any more heartache.

It now is Kroenke's baby, who also owns the Rams, the Denver Nuggets of the NBA, the Colorado Avalanche of the NHL, the Colorado Rapids of MLS and the Arsenal of the Premier League.

Kroenke, who tried to buy the Dodgers a decade ago, is expected to keep the Angels in Anaheim, and expand his footprint across the Los Angeles and Orange County landscape.

"The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market," Kroenke said in a statement. "We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization."

So do their fans, who now will start dreaming of a day that Trout returns to the postseason before his Hall of Fame career ends.

Maybe, Anaheim once again can be the "Happiest Place on Earth."

On the mound, Jacob Misiorowski owns a 1.73 ERA with 222 strikeouts in 151 innings. If he can stay below 2.00 and reach 250 strikeouts, he would be the first pitcher to accomplish both since Jacob deGrom in 2018.

title: Hall of Famer survived Yankees owner George Steinbrenner: ’I'll never reclaim those years'
description: MLB legend Dave Winfield is hoping to inspire others to stand strong with his new book.
fullText:
New Yankees owner George Steinbrenner tried everything to break him and destroy his reputation to the point of no return, but Dave Winfield refused to let him win.

Winfield stood up to the most powerful owner in baseball, fought back just like he has throughout life, and now proudly tells his story with a book – and soon, a documentary.

It will not attract splashy headlines and have the internet buzzing. It won't make former teammates and managers uncomfortable with secrets that are unveiled. It instead provides a deep emotional dive into the man himself.

Winfield insisted from the start of the hour-long interview with USA TODAY Sports that for everyone who thinks they really know him, once you read "Touching All the Bases: A Story of Power, Purpose, and Surviving the Bronx," you'll find out that you really didn't know him.

Winfield poured his heart and soul into the book, which was nearly six years in the making, and will be released Sept. 15.

He talks about life as a Black athlete going against one of the most powerful men in sports in Steinbrenner, details the heartache and stress of court battles with a woman from his past, the pain of the George Floyd murder in Minneapolis across the river where he grew up in St. Paul, working in the players union and his frustration with former players who are part of commissioner Rob Manfred's ambassador program, performance-enhancing drugs, personal tragedy, his bout with prostate cancer, his philanthropic foundation, flying out of New York City the morning of the terrorist attacks and his heartbreaking trip to Ground Zero.

"I've had a unique life, legacy and experience, and I have a unique story to tell," Winfield says. "My life experience is so different than what most people would imagine. I'm in the seventh inning of life, so it's time to tell it.

"If you've got a unique experience or story, I believe you've got to share it with people."

The experience, as he details in his book: "My experience as a Black man who went to war with one of the most powerful owners in sports tells an essential story, not just about the triumphs and challenges of my own career, but about the dynamics of race and power in America."

Winfield, 74, isn't comparing himself to Jackie Robinson or Curt Flood, but no one else comes to mind in the past 50 years in baseball who was more tormented and mistreated, but courageously fought back, becoming a first-ballot Hall of Fame player and one of the most well-respected athletes in the sports world.

He survived Steinbrenner's attempts to bring ruin him, but in the end, it was Steinbrenner who went down, receiving a lifetime suspension that was reduced to 2 ½ years for hiring a gambler in a failed attempt to destroy Winfield's reputation.

"I could have been really vengeful, hateful, disrespectful, unhappy, for all of the things that were thrown at me," Winfield says. "But that never happened. I won't say I didn't have bruises and was bent a little bit, but I didn't break.

"When I think about my career, people will say was quite successful, but I don't really know how good I could have been at the pinnacle of my career if I had been supported. I think I would have been a better player."

It was when the world was shut down from COVID in 2020 that Winfield was home, watching the horrifying footage of George Floyd being strangled on the streets by a Minneapolis police officer, that he knew it was time to tell his story.

"I had something that George Floyd and so many other Black people didn't," Winfield writes, "a voice. A chance to speak, to be heard, and to defend myself. Too many people don't have that chance. I hope those coming up today keep the pressure on our leaders and stand alongside the 'old heads' who have fought through past struggles for equality.

"I hope they refuse to relent too soon and push tirelessly for real transformation."

Winfield can't wait now to meet and shake the hands of Kwanza Jones, who became the first Black majority owner of a baseball team when she and her husband, Jose E. Feliciano, purchased the San Diego Padres, his first team. It has been a long time coming, but finally, history was made.

"It would have been nice to see it sooner,'' Winfield says, "but it doesn't surprise me that it hasn't happened before now. I'm just happy it has happened now."

Winfield, who once was interested in being part of an ownership group himself, has plenty to share to whoever wants to listen. No other player in baseball history had such a highly publicized feud with his team owner, and lived to tell about it, with the owner being the one who was suspended from the game.

It was nasty. It was revolting. It was public.

"Those disputes weren't just about money," said Winfield, who signed a historic 10-year, $23 million contract with the Yankees, "they were about power. It was an owner, speaking for all the others, making sure a player knew his place."

Despite years without speaking after his departure, with Steinbrenner irate and canceling plans to retire his number after Winfield chose to wear a Padres cap cap into the Hall of Fame, Winfield's wife, Tonya, convinced him to see Steinbrenner perhaps for the final time. Winfield took a six-hour flight to Tampa in July 2008, two years before Steinbrenner died.

"I decided to make the trip," Winfield said, "hoping it might help quite some of the angry thought that had been pin-balling around my head for decades. …. When I saw him, it was clear he wasn't well. His handshake had weakened. He struggled for words and could barely speak above a whisper. I could see he didn't have the strength or clarity to have an in-depth conversation about our past."

They spoke for 90 minutes. It started with a handshake. It ended with a hug.

"Did the meeting give me a sense of reconciliation, closure, or validation?" Winfield said. "To some extent it did, but I'll never reclaim those years of anguish.''

Winfield, who spent 12 years as a special assistant in the players union before retiring last spring, is proud of playing a major role with the union. He has seen the union's power evolve from the first time he put on his first MLB uniform 53 years ago, going straight from the University of Minnesota to the big leagues with the Padres.

There was no free agency in 1973. No salary arbitration. The minimum salary was $16,000. Most players had second jobs in the winter.

Now, the average MLB salary is $5.34 million, with two players – Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani – receiving free-agent contracts worth at least $700 million. Winfield made about $28 million his entire career, which is $32 million less than Dodgers right fielder Kyle Tucker is earning just this year.

"I expect the owners will do whatever necessary to get what they want," Winfield writes, "including fighting dirty and impugning reputations. I know from personal experience how dirty the fight can get. We must stand strong in defense of our hard-earned rights."

Winfield, the first of four Hall of Famers from his hometown of St. Paul – with Jack Morris, Paul Molitor and Joe Mauer – talks about being a proud Minnesotan, where he was honored in May with St. Paul erecting a statue of him in the Dunning Sports Complex. He played every sport growing up, and was drafted by four teams in three sports in 1973. The Padres selected him with the fourth pick in the draft, the fifth round by the Atlanta Hawks of the NBA and the sixth round by the Utah Stars in the ABA, and the Minnesota Vikings in the 17th round.

"Believe me, I tell many parents now to allow your kids to play other sports," Winfield said. "You're seeing these kids get injured or burnt out by playing one sport. Coaches want to dominate all of their time with one sport. Let them be kids."

Winfield, who begins his book tour on Sept. 8 with an appearance on "Good Morning America'' and "The View'' the following day, hopes that his book and an upcoming documentary will help inspire those facing their own adversity.

"I'm an outlier how you approach things in life,'' Winfield says. "I've never been afraid to travel, go outside, never afraid to meet new people. There are a lot of people that would roll up in a ball and quit if they faced all the negative stuff coming my way. I overcame really significant odds, ugly situations and a lot of adversity. I went through it all and came out Ok on the other end.

"Hopefully, people can be empowered, motivated and uplifted what I have written.''

title: MLB Attempts To Tie Limited Free Agent Signing Period To Competitive Balance
description: MLB offered a new proposal as part of the latest collective bargaining sessions that would create a limited free agent signing period, but only contingent on a salary cap.
fullText:
On Thursday, Major League Baseball made its latest proposal to the MLB Players Association for the next collective bargaining agreement. It would create an extreme shift in the free agent signing period, looking to mirror other sports by placing a strict limit on the window in which signings could take place, creating a frenzied period designed to increase fan interest.

As first reported by MLB.com, the five days after the World Series would still allow players and clubs to trigger or decline options. After that, free agents would be allowed to negotiate deals, but signings would only be allowed after 12 p.m. on the Monday of the first day of the Winter Meetings through December 21st. From Dec. 21st through the first Monday in February, no free agent signings or trades would be allowed. After the first Monday in February, free agent signings would then be allowed to resume.

It is not the first time that the league has sought to have a limited free agent signing period. The league proposed it as part of the negotiations of the current labor deal in place since 2021, and as recently as January, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred discussed it on WFAN, touting it as a way to promote excitement.

"I think there's going to be some more conversation about it, because I do believe that there's a marketing opportunity," Manfred said. "Let's face it, we operate in a really competitive environment. Just put entertainment, generally, to one side — just sports, right? It's really competitive. And I think that you make a mistake, particularly during the offseason, when you don't take every advantage to push your sport out in front of your fans during that down period."

An important change in direction with the latest proposal is that the league has suddenly shifted and is tying it to implementing a salary cap. That was not the case in negotiations for the current labor deal, nor did Manfred mention it on WFAN in January.

When asked why the proposal on Thursday could not be offered separately from MLB's push for a cap system, MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said, "In our current economic system, these changes would be too harmful to competitive balance and would not be practical."

As The Athletic reported in January, player agents see the limited signing period differently.

Scott Boras, who has notoriously used the start of Spring Training to leverage deals for his players, sees the proposal negatively.

"The sole purpose of deadlines (is to) simply restrict competition and deny players the true market," Boras said. "Our current rules allow for ultimate roster construction and the best possible team for a season. (A deadline is) not for competition reasons. Every owner wants the opportunity for time to allow him to respond to changes by his competitors. That's why there's been many significant signings 

Other agents, notably Joel Wolfe, head of the Wasserman's baseball division, have seen limited signing windows work with international players from Japan.

"If there was a way to re-create the exceptional efficiency of the posting system for all the free agents, I would certainly be interested in that," said Wolfe, who represents Los Angeles Dodgers pitchers Roki Sasaki and Yoshinobu Yamamoto to The Athletic. "But I have yet to see a good answer as to what happens to the FA's if they go unsigned that doesn't unfairly prejudice them. MLB teams always seem to find a way to game the system and crush a large part of the class. I think it's worth exploring.

"I just haven't seen any great idea yet that benefits all the players."

The proposal on Thursday to limit the free agent signing period and tie it to the cap system garnered a pointed response from MLBPA interim Executive Director, Bruce Meyer.

"The league, through their propaganda arm, is promoting their latest set of roster and transaction proposals as player-friendly," said Meyer. "MLB expressly conditioned these proposals on the players' agreement to a salary cap system, which would drastically reduce overall player compensation, eliminate fully guaranteed contracts through escrow, and turn back the clock on fundamental player rights."

"Their latest proposals regarding free agency would eliminate Player rights by establishing an artificial free agency window, subject to a salary cap, which would reduce player leverage and create a game of musical chairs pitting player vs. player."

"The suggestion that the only way to limit roster churn, or incentivize earlier Free Agent signings is with a salary cap is entirely unserious. Players have proposed changes that would address these priorities, but the league is not interested in any changes that don't directly reduce the rights of all players and shift leverage to the owners."

The current labor deal between MLB and the players is set to expire at 11:59 pm ET on December 1st. If the owners and players do not agree on a new deal by then, the owners are expected to lock out the players. If so, the Baseball Winter Meetings would be canceled, and all player transactions – either trades or free agent signings – would stop until a new labor deal is reached.

The 2027 MLB regular season is scheduled to start on the night of Wednesday, March 24th.

title: Tommy John, longtime MLB pitcher and namesake of baseball's most important surgery, dies at 83
description: Tommy John and Dr. Frank Jobe changed baseball from an operating room in 1974.
fullText:
Tommy John, the namesake and first recipient of baseball's most important surgery, died on Sunday, the New York Yankees announced. He was 83 years old.

John was reported to be entering hospice in early August, two years after he announced a battle with bladder cancer. He took the occasion to pen a goodbye letter to fans and other acquaintances on the day of the New York Yankees' Old-Timers' Day, where he was a frequent participant.

"While his incredible longevity and post-surgery achievements changed the fortunes and trajectory of countless athletes around the world, it also overshadowed his excellence as a pitcher, which included consecutive 20‑win seasons with the Yankees," the team's statement read. "We pause to remember the totality of his legacy — his competitiveness and skill, his penchant for conversation, his kind and gracious nature, and his stature as an athletic and medical pioneer."

Thanks to the surgery, John's career spanned 27 years, appearing for six different teams and racking up 288 wins. Only 25 pitchers in MLB history have more wins, and only two — known steroid user Roger Clemens and dead-ball era star Bobby Mathews — are not enshrined in the National Baseball Hall of Fame.

John remains a notable exclusion from Cooperstown, between his successful career and presence in the operating room that changed baseball.

STATEMENT FROM THE NEW YORK YANKEES:

“The New York Yankees mourn the passing of Tommy John, who was a bedrock of our rotation during his time in pinstripes and a longtime favorite of Yankees fans. While his incredible longevity and post-surgery achievements changed the fortunes… pic.twitter.com/p6ndlBxUTb

Before 1974, a torn UCL was an unrecoverable blow for a pitcher's career, with treatment usually consisting of some combination of rest, painkillers and prayer. That appeared to be John's fate after July 17, 1974, when the Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander felt something pop in his arm during the third inning of a start against the Montreal Expos.

As recalled in a comment documented by the Society for American Baseball Research:

"Right at the point where I put force on the pitch, the point where my arm is back and bent, something happened," he explained. "It felt as if I had left my arm someplace else. It was as if my body continued to go forward and my left arm had just flown out to right field, independent of the rest of me."

The eventual diagnosis was a torn UCL, and the man tasked with treating John was Dodgers team physician Dr. Frank Jobe. As Jobe recalled in "The Arm" by Jeff Passan, his advice to John was straightforward: "We just told him to go home … he was through playing baseball."

John, however, was desperate. He was 31 years old and had been a successful pitcher for the Dodgers, Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Indians across 12 seasons up to that point. He did not want that career to end and pressed Jobe for a possible fix.

Jobe's answer was to use a surgery that had been in use for years, just never on elbows. He would take a tendon from John's right wrist and put it in his left elbow, to replace a UCL that turned out to be fully ruptured. He told John there was a 1% chance it would work, but later admitted to Passan that was to avoid false hope. He was pretty sure it could work.

It worked, and the results speak for themselves. After an arduous rehab process that ate his 1975 season, John returned to the mound and went on to play 14 more seasons in the big leagues. He had 124 wins with his first UCL and 164 with its replacement. One All-Star nod with the first and three the replacement. Zero career Cy Young votes, then two runner-up finishes.

John's penultimate season saw him lead the Yankees in starts with 32 at the age of 45. When he retired in 1989, he had tied Deacon McGuire's modern-era MLB record for seasons played with 26, which was later broken by Nolan Ryan.

There is no procedure in the history of sports medicine that has altered a sport so drastically. Modern baseball and its high-octane arms are unthinkable without Tommy John surgery. Among the 10 pitchers to receive votes for the American League Cy Young Award in 2025, eight have undergone the UCL repair named after its first recipient.

Rather than being a career-ender, news of a torn UCL is now essentially received as if the pitcher has been put in timeout for a year. The expectation is he will come back, though there are unfortunately still a few exceptions due to surgery complications. The risk is so minimized these days that there have been reports of horrendously misguided parents volunteering their young pitchers for a new UCL because they think it means a potential velocity bump.

Jobe, who died in 2014, deserves the lion's share of the credit for what the surgery has done, but it took a pushy patient to get him there.

title: 6 NBA teams screwed over by the schedule release
description: The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. NHL calendars lean heavily on divisional matchups and regional rivalries. MLB moved to a more balanced schedule in […]
fullText:
The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. An NFL team that finishes in first place in their division one year draws other first-place teams on the schedule the next year. NHL calendars lean heavily on divisional matchups and regional rivalries. MLB moved to a more balanced schedule in 2023, reducing the number of division games and increasing interleague play to even things out.

The NBA does not play a balanced schedule, but the biggest factor in an individual team's success often feels like it has more to do with the travel arrangements than who they're playing on a particular night. Trimming the NBA's 82-game regular season schedule always felt like a silver bullet for many of the league's most pressing problems. Until that happens, teams are still jetting around the country every night to try to sell out as many arenas as possible.

The 2026-27 NBA schedule came out this week. Read our take on the league's 10 biggest rivalries for the upcoming season. With a little help from Shamit Dua's NBA Schedule Dash Board, these are the teams who got hit the hardest by the schedule makers this year.

The Celtics' 16 back-to-backs are in a five-way tie for the most in the NBA. They play 22 times in a stretch of three games in four nights, which ranks as the eighth hardest in the league. They are -4 in "net rest" games, which measures who the more tired opponent is in a given game. The Celtics aren't just dealing with the loss of Jaylen Brown this season, they're also needing to navigate one of the league's hardest travel schedules. I still think the Celtics will be a regular season wins machine, and I wouldn't count them out for grabbing the No. 1 seed in the East, but the road to get there looks more daunting after the schedule release.

The Pelicans have the hardest schedule in the NBA this year. New Orleans plays a league-leading 16 back-to-backs, they're the only team in the NBA with 27 'three in four nights' stretches, and they have a -5 net rest disadvantage. The Pelicans already had the league's seventh-lowest over/under at 29.5 wins coming into the season, and it feels like it's going to be an uphill climb to even hit that number. New head coach Jamahl Mosley has his work cut out for him. After years of believing in Zion Williamson, I'm finally giving up the dream that he can be one of the NBA's best players. At this point, I'm more interested in seeing what Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen can do together.

The Bulls are one of the league-leaders with 15 back-to-backs this season. They play a stretch of three games in four nights 24 times, which is the fourth most in the league. They're -3 on "net rest," which is third-hardest in the league. The Bulls also have five time zone crossings on no rest, which is the fifth-most in the league. The first 15 games of the season are especially brutal for Chicago, with two games against Boston, two games against the Knicks, two games against the Sixers, and one game each vs. San Antonio, Minnesota, and Cleveland. The Bulls are starting yet another rebuild, but it's going to be difficult for this fanbase to be patient when the team has the third worst cumulative record in the NBA after the last nine seasons. This year is more about figuring out if they have a future star in Caleb Wilson, and seeing how Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey develop in their third year together. The Bulls actually have a decent bench led by Leonard Miller, Jalen Smith, and Tre Jones, and they're going to need it with this type of schedule.

The Cavs missed out on LeBron James and got a tough schedule to boot. Cleveland is tied for the league-lead with 16 back-to-backs. They have 23 'three in four nights' games, which is the sixth hardest in the NBA. They're a -2 in rest advantage, also sixth hardest. The Cavs have done a whole lot of nothing this summer coming off the world's least convincing conference finals run, but there's still time to potentially land Peyton Watson or swing a big trade. I just get the sense that Cleveland's Eastern Conference rivals are passing them by … unless Evan Mobley has another leap left in him.

The Mavericks have 16 back-to-backs (tied for the most in the league), and they're at a -3 net rest advantage. It will be fascinating to see how Dallas manages Kyrie Irving as he returns from a torn ACL at age-34. The team will also have to manage Dereck Lively II, because the 22-year-old big man still hasn't been cleared to run after having foot surgery in December. I could see a world where Cooper Flagg takes a big leap and carries the Mavs to playoff contention, but it's important to remember Flagg won't turn 20 years old until just before Christmas. It might be wise for Dallas' new front office to take a more long-term view around their franchise star.

The Lakers play 15 back-to-backs. They face three games in four nights 26 times, which is the second most in the league. There's so much riding on Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves this year. Both of them dealt with injuries last year, playing 115 out of a possible 164 games. That's not going to cut it this year. Doncic and Reaves need to carry this offense every night without LeBron James around, and the Lakers probably don't want to know what happens when Quentin Grimes needs to be their first or second option for a night. Will the Lakers have a plan to save Luka in some back-to-backs? It's going to be a battle in the Western Conference every night, but the Lakers really just need him healthy for the playoffs, unlike last year.

For a whole three-game series to happen at Field of Dreams, there would need to be more permanent housing available in the area. Dyersville is a town of just over 4,300 people and about 70 miles from any interstate highway.

To build more hotels and other lodging would be excellent as far as a potential game/series goes. However, that could end up compromising the charm of the town and game atmosphere.

For now, it is just the one-off game before the teams return to one of their parks to host the rest of the series. The Phillies and Twins will play two more at Target Field in Minneapolis on Saturday night and Sunday afternoon.

The Philadelphia Phillies are coming off a series loss to the St. Louis Cardinals, but they'll have a quick turnaround Thursday.

They're set to face the Minnesota Twins in the third-ever Field of Dreams Game, which MLB created around the iconic Kevin Costner baseball movie Field of Dreams.

The game will take place in Dyersville, Iowa, at a custom-built ballpark next to the cornfield featured in the 1989 movie.

Ahead of the matchup, MLB allowed each team to add a 27th player to its roster for the game. The Phillies announced their addition just hours before first pitch after releasing their lineup.

Philadelphia added 28-year-old outfielder Kameron Misner from Triple-A Lehigh Valley as its extra player for the game. He'll wear No. 18.

Misner is a left-handed hitter with major league experience, having appeared in 97 career games across three seasons with the Tampa Bay Rays and Royals.

Misner has struggled since joining the Phillies' minor league system, batting just .195 in 12 games. However, he has put together a solid 2026 Triple-A campaign overall, appearing in 75 games and posting a .900 OPS.

title: Tarp comes off at Field of Dreams as MLB officials hope rain holds off
description: The rain, for now, has stopped. Whether it stays that way is the question hanging over Major League Baseball’s return to the Field of Dreams.
fullText:
DYERSVILLE — The tarp is off. The rain, for now, has stopped.

Whether it stays that way is the question hanging over Major League Baseball's return to the Field of Dreams.

Around 1 p.m. Thursday, Aug. 13, crews began uncovering the diamond at the Dubuque County ballpark after a soggy morning and early afternoon, the first real break from hours of rain ahead of the Minnesota Twins' 6:30 p.m. CT game against the Philadelphia Phillies.

Workers hauled sandbags from the edges of the tarp before lining up across the outfield and wrapping the massive sheet around a long, black corrugated pipe. A swarm of groundskeepers then spread out with leaf blowers and rakes, clearing puddles and working the dirt beneath a gloomy, gray sky.

An MLB staffer told the Register that the tarp came off so crews could begin rehearsals ahead of the game. There was no assurance the break in the weather would last.

"All fingers are crossed," the staffer said.

A round of showers and thunderstorms moved across most of Iowa on Thursday morning, with heavy rain and strong winds among the concerns. Forecasters expected the most widespread rain earlier in the day and some improvement by early afternoon, although scattered showers could linger.

As of shortly after 1 p.m., the rain had stopped at the Field of Dreams Movie Site. But the hourly forecast still called for rain in Dyersville through much of the afternoon and early evening, including around the scheduled first pitch.

The changing conditions were built into Thursday's preparations.

As the grounds crew worked below, the outfield scoreboard cycled through rehearsal messages for an array of possible weather emergencies. One would instruct fans to seek shelter from lightning. Another would tell fans to return to their vehicles if severe weather delayed the opening of the gates. Other test messages covered a weather delay, an evacuation, a cancellation and a postponement of the game until Friday.

title: Dodgers' Freddie Freeman somehow avoids serious injury in frightening fall into visitors' dugout
description: Freddie Freeman apparently avoided serious injury Wednesday night when the Los Angeles Dodgers' first baseman took a frightening tumble down the stairs and into the visitors' dugout while trying to catch a foul popup in the eighth inning.  Freeman isn't sure whether he'll play when the Dodgers begin an important four-game series with the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday, but he's grateful his freefall to the dugout floor wasn't worse.  “I didn't hit my head, so that was the key part there,” Freeman said.
fullText:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Freddie Freeman apparently avoided serious injury Wednesday night when the Los Angeles Dodgers' first baseman took a frightening tumble down the stairs and into the visitors' dugout while trying to catch a foul popup in the eighth inning.

Freeman isn't sure whether he'll play when the Dodgers begin an important four-game series with the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday, but he's grateful his freefall to the dugout floor wasn't worse.

"I didn't hit my head, so that was the key part there," Freeman said. "I am sore. Kneecaps are sore. Shoulder is sore. Hand sore. Wrist sore. I mean, I fell. (But) I'm in good spirits."

Freeman stayed in the game and finished the top of the eighth, but Tommy Edman pinch hit for him in the bottom of the inning before Los Angeles closed out a 4-2 victory over the Kansas City Royals, its fourth in five games.

The right side of Freeman's body took the punishment, but the 2024 World Series MVP apparently didn't break any bones. He'll wait to see how he feels in the morning before he decides whether to play Thursday night when the back-to-back World Series champion Dodgers welcome Milwaukee in a reamtch of last year's National League Championship Series.

Freeman said he simply miscalculated the location of the dugout railing while he tracked Isaac Collins' foul pop.

"I went to lean, like I was going to lean against the rail to catch the ball — and obviously there was no rail," Freeman said with a smile.

Freeman, who turns 37 in one month, said he was fortunate to fall all the way into the dugout, missing the top flight of stairs entirely. That's because when he landed, his head stuck out into the open space above the second flight of stairs that goes down into the visitors' clubhouse instead of banging on the ground.

"Luckily, I was tall, so I missed everything else," the 6-foot-4 Freeman cracked.

This wasn't Freeman's first fielding misadventure: He said he fell into the seats in Arizona roughly a decade ago while he was with the Atlanta Braves.

The Orange County native and childhood Angels fan also said he still remembers the infamous 1999 opening-day dugout fall by Mo Vaughn, who got hurt on the first play of his first game with the Halos.

The Royals rushed to Freeman's side after the fall, urging him to stay on the ground. Freeman decided to get up anyway, and the Dodgers' training staff rushed across the field to check on him.

"I think that we really dodged a bullet," Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts said. "Very scary visually. For right now, he's in good spirits, which I think is a good sign. Just kind of total body soreness."

SAN DIEGO (AP) — Jackson Merrill hit a tying sacrifice fly in the 11th inning and Luis Campusano followed with a two-out single to bring in Sun-Mung Song from second base as the San Diego Padres beat the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 on Wednesday for a three-game sweep.

The surging Padres have won five straight and 15 of 19 to move into the National League's second wild-card spot ahead of Arizona and Philadelphia.

Gary Sánchez doubled home the go-ahead run for Milwaukee off Adrian Morejon (9-2) in the top of the 11th.

Merrill tied it when his sac fly off Antonio Senzatela (9-4) brought in automatic runner Jake Cronenworth. Song, who pinch ran after Ty France was hit by a pitch, stole second before Campusano punched an opposite-field single to right. Luis Lara's throw home was high, allowing Song to slide in headfirst with the winning run.

The Padres tied the game at 2 with two outs in the eighth when Fernando Tatis Jr. raced around from second base to score on Cronenworth's infield single.

Cronenworth hit a bouncer to first baseman Jake Bauers, who flipped it to reliever Aaron Ashby but he was late covering first and Cronenworth beat him to the bag for an RBI single. Ashby turned toward home but didn't make a throw as Tatis sprinted in with the tying run.

Dustin May pitched brilliantly into the eighth for the Brewers. He allowed one run and four hits, struck out six and walked two. He gave up Xander Bogaerts' homer in the third.

Sánchez, who was with the Padres for part of the 2023 season, homered to left field against Robbie Ray in the second.

Brewers LHP Shane Drohan (6-4, 3.87 ERA) is scheduled to start opposite Dodgers RHP Roki Sasaki (5-5, 4.54) on Thursday in the opener of a four-game series in Los Angeles.

Padres RHP Michael King (7-8, 3.37 ERA) is set to start Friday in the opener of a three-game series at Cleveland, which counters with RHP Gavin Williams (11-6, 3.55).

title: Alex Rodriguez: The Dodgers are ‘great’ for baseball
description: While some fans and media believe the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining Major League Baseball, Alex Rodriguez appears to be a fan of their spending. After admitting he voted in Awful Announcing’s 2026 MLB local TV announcer rankings during an appearance on The Michael Kay Show on ESPN New York, the discussion turned to the…
fullText:
While some fans and media believe the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining Major League Baseball, Alex Rodriguez appears to be a fan of their spending.

After admitting he voted in Awful Announcing's 2026 MLB local TV announcer rankings during an appearance on The Michael Kay Show on ESPN New York, the discussion turned to the current state of the Yankees, who have been ravaged by injuries and offensive struggles. And while the Yankees remain favorites to win the American League pennant, Kay asked Rodriguez about their biggest potential hurdle to a World Series.

The rich got richer at the trade deadline, when the Dodgers added two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. It reignited conversations about whether the Dodgers are good for baseball or will end up driving owners to continue their push for a hard salary cap during the current labor negotiations. And after Kay held firm that the Dodgers are good for baseball, Rodriguez agreed.

"I think it's great. You and I both would be hypocrites if we said it's not good when we saw what happened in the '90s here in New York, what happened in '09 when Hal Steinbrenner flexed his financial resources to go out and get CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett and the year before we had Johnny Damon," Rodriguez told Kay.

Rodriguez noted that the key to spending money is not making mistakes, suggesting that the $22 million the Yankees spent on outfielder Trent Grisham may have been a mistake. Similarly, the Dodgers shelled out massive contracts for Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in the offseason, which have yet to pan out.

As a former player, current broadcaster and franchise owner, albeit in the NBA with the Minnesota Timberwolves, Rodriguez is in a unique position to weigh in on the Dodgers. It's hard for Rodriguez to be against the Dodgers flexing their resources considering he signed a groundbreaking 10-year, $252 million contract with the Texas Rangers in 2000 before playing for the Yankees during their peak spending era. It would also be hard for Rodriguez to rant against a salary cap, given that he's an NBA owner with a soft cap.

If the Dodgers win their third World Series in a row after adding Skubal to a star-studded roster highlighted by Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, and Freddie Freeman, the calls for MLB to fix its financial imbalance will grow as they head toward a lockout. But the Dodgers' ability to play the role of the villain also undoubtedly makes the playoffs more compelling, which is why they're still great for baseball.

fullText:
In just his second full season at the major league level, Athletics shortstop Jacob Wilson is already making MLB history.

On Sunday night, as the Athletics picked up a series win over the Boston Red Sox, Wilson played in his 111th straight game without recording an error. By doing so, he surpassed former Athletic Mike Bordick's 24 year old record for the longest errorless streak by a shortstop in the history of Major League Baseball. Bordick set the record at the age of 36 during the 2002 season while a member of the Baltimore Orioles and finished the season with just a single error.

"[I'm] a little surprised that record got broken," Bordick said on MLB Network Radio. "That young man is picking it out there as an Athletic."

"It's a special day for me, but at the end of the day, we got our first series win in a long time against a great opponent," Wilson told MLB.com's Greg Levinsky.

Ironically, Bordick's sole error in the 2002 season was on April 10, 2002, less than two weeks after Wilson was born on March 30. As for Wilson, his most recent error came more than a calendar year ago. He had a single error on July 6, 2025 against the Athletics' Northern California rival, the San Francisco Giants. It was his eighth error of his rookie season.

During the 2026 season, Wilson has had 81 putouts and 128 assists, along with 28 double plays, yet has been perfect to this point.

Wilson, 24, has been limited to just 76 of the Athletics' 118 games this year due to injury, but when in the lineup, he's been one of their  most reliable bats as well. His .269 batting average is the most among any Athletic to appear in more than 70 games to this point in the season and the second-highest amongst any player to appear in more than 20 games, trailing just Zack Gelof's .273 average.

It's been a big year for Wilson, both on and off of the field, as he signed a huge contract extension to stay with the Athletics back in February. His new contract runs through the 2032 season and is worth a total of $70 million. title: Hagen Smith, Colson Montgomery Lead White Sox to Series Win Over Guardians
description: Hagen Smith delivered two scoreless innings in his MLB debut, while Colson Montgomery’s three-run homer lifted the White Sox to a crucial series win.
fullText:
It will be the division games that matter most for the Chicago White Sox down the stretch of the 2026 season. And after suffering another difficult-to-stomach sweep at the hands of the Boston Red Sox, the White Sox answered with a big weekend series win over the Cleveland Guardians.

It all came down to Sunday's rubber match, when Davis Martin took the ball and surrendered two runs in the first inning before being removed from the game following a rain delay that lasted more than two hours.

The early stages of the game did not set up well for Chicago. While the offense jumped on Joey Cantillo with three consecutive hits to start the game, the White Sox left two runners in scoring position with nobody out in the bottom of the first inning. They then immediately went into the rain delay trailing 2-1, knowing their starting pitcher would be done for the day after recording just three outs.

That was a big blow for a White Sox team with an already taxed bullpen, one that had been pushed to the limit Thursday night in Boston during a 13-inning defeat. But with a key off day coming Monday, manager Will Venable emptied the tank, and the White Sox relievers proved up to the task. That included left-handed pitcher Hagen Smith, the No. 2 prospect in the White Sox organization, who made his MLB debut Sunday.

Smith's debut was true to form. He recorded his first MLB strikeout on three pitches against Brayan Rocchio, the first batter he faced. He struck out the side in his first inning of work, even managing to punch out the notoriously stingy Steven Kwan.

Smith's second inning, however, was much tougher. He walked three batters to load the bases with two outs, then worked a full count against Rocchio before inducing a lineout to third baseman Miguel Vargas. Smith escaped the jam despite issuing four walks on the day, ultimately throwing two scoreless innings and earning the win in his first MLB appearance.

He got that win thanks to Colson Montgomery, who stepped up with two runners on and two outs in the bottom of the third inning and pummeled a Craig Yoho pitch 110.7 mph for his 26th home run of the year. That blast put the White Sox on top 5-2, a lead they held for the rest of the afternoon.

The Colson Montgomery haters are in SHAMBLES!#WhiteSox lead 5-2 on his 26th home run. pic.twitter.com/zz9rq3tqqt

It was an impressive display by the White Sox, who picked themselves up off the mat following a rough start to the game. Both the offense and the pitching staff did enough to secure the win.

"We all stayed pretty much locked in," Montgomery said of the rain delay during his postgame interview with Brooke Fletcher. "We treated it like a whole new ballgame, 0-0."

That win gives the White Sox their largest division lead of the season. It also put a new team in Chicago's rearview mirror. The White Sox now hold a 3.5 game lead in the AL Central, and it is the red-hot Detroit Tigers who sit in second place, with Cleveland and Minnesota both 4.0 games back.

The Tigers are 7-2 over their last nine games. It's an ironic time for a hot streak after they traded both Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize at the MLB trade deadline, but they are by no means out of the race. The White Sox will have to keep taking care of business and stacking series wins if they want to run away with the AL Central crown.

A series win over the Guardians was a good start, but the difficult tests are not over. Next weekend, the White Sox will travel to Detroit for a three-game series against the Tigers.
