fullText:
The Athletics have parted ways with former general manager David Forst after a season in which the team has struggled to win games.

With a 45-70 record this season, the Athletics have been one of the biggest disappointments in all of MLB. Armed with a load of young, talented, and controllable players, things have seemingly fallen apart for the Athletics, who were supposed to contend for the playoffs this season. Instead, the team is battling the Los Angeles Angels for last place in the American League West, and it cost Forst his job.

The Athletics confirmed in a statement that they have parted ways with Forst, with assistant general manager Dan Feinstein taking over on an interim basis for the rest of 2026.

"David has been an integral part of the A's and our success for nearly three decades. His leadership, dedication, and commitment to this team have helped shape our baseball operations department and position us for the future. We are grateful for everything David has done for our organization," said A's owner and managing partner John Fisher in a statement posted on the team's website.

Forst also spoke after leaving the team that he has spent the last 27 years with, offering a classy statement after exiting the organization.

"It was truly an honor to spend the last 27 years with the A's, especially the last 11 as the GM. This organization is full of incredibly talented, devoted, and good people, and I am lucky to have worked alongside them for so long," Forst said.

The 50-year-old Forst was first hired by the A's in 2000, when he worked as a scout for the team. He then became the team's assistant general manager to Billy Beane in 2004 and was then promoted to general manager in 2015 after Beane left his post.

The Athletics won the AL West just once during Forst's 10 seasons as the team's GM, in 2020, and only made the playoffs three times.

With the team slated to move to Las Vegas for 2028, they will have a new front office in place.

The Mets reliever recorded the first strikeout of his major league career Wednesday night against the Cleveland Guardians, freezing pinch hitter Angel Martinez on an 88.7 mph slider in the sixth inning of New York's eventual 6-5 win.

Asked afterward to grade the execution of his signature celebration, Yan did not hold back.

Cleveland fans booed him off the mound, a reaction Yan said did not bother him in the slightest.

"Honestly, I don't think about that," Yan said. "They can do whatever they want there. They're paying their tickets, so if they want to yell at me, if they want to boo me, they can do whatever they want. I'm in my zone, and I'm going to enjoy my game any way that I want to."

Yan's path to this moment took over a decade. Originally signed by the Los Angeles Angels out of the Dominican Republic in 2014, he spent years bouncing around the minors, including a stretch working as a roofer in Arizona to make ends meet, before a stint in Japan and later Colorado's system.

He signed a minor league deal with the Mets last August and was called up from Triple-A Syracuse on Monday, finally debuting at age 29 with the same electric celebration that had already made him a viral sensation in spring training.

Interim manager Andy Green praised the moment for what it represented beyond just the strikeout itself.

"It's real stuff. It's really impressive. To get out of a bases-loaded jam, get your first punchout, just excited for him. He deserves that," Green said.

title: MLB Trade Grades: A’s Have Quiet Trade Deadline
description: Should the team have done more?
fullText:
While nearly every other MLB team made moves at the 2026 MLB trade deadline to boost its present and future, the Athletics sat on the sidelines, unwilling to shake up a roster that is staring down a fifth straight losing season.

Entering the deadline, it felt like the A's were not going to do much, as the organization continues building in anticipation of its 2028 relocation to Las Vegas. As such, it made sense that the team kept recently extended starters Jacob Wilson and Tyler Soderstrom off the market, as well as promising rookies Henry Bolte, Gage Jump and Joshua Kuroda-Grauer.

The reason why the team did basically nothing was that it had no healthy, valuable players to put on the trade block. Injuries and performance regression were major factors behind the team's collapse over the past couple of months.

The A's two pending free-agents, left-handed pitcher Jeffrey Springs and second baseman Jeff McNeil, stayed with the team. Their poor performances and team-options for next season likely discouraged contending teams from pursuing them.

The Athletics' lone move was announced right at the deadline. The club traded 25-year-old outfielder Colby Thomas to the Philadelphia Phillies in exchange for right-handed reliever Seth Johnson.

Thomas had plenty of opportunity to prove himself with the Athletics since he made his MLB debut last August, but he failed to provide much of an impact. With the A's, he accumulated 10 home runs and 30 RBIs over his first 234 major league at-bats. Now he goes to Philadelphia, where he will look to provide some thump against left-handed pitchers for a Phillies team in the postseason hunt.

Johnson can immediately slot into an A's bullpen in need of help. Through 16 appearances with the Phillies this season, the hard-throwing 27-year-old recorded a 1-0 record, a 5.51 ERA and 20 strikeouts. He has fared significantly better at Triple-A, going 1-1 with a 2.17 ERA at that lower level.

They traded from a position of strength, getting rid of Thomas, who projects as only a platoon bat due to the incompetence he has shown against right-handed pitchers. In return, they acquired a former highly ranked pitching prospect who could help a bullpen that owns the worst ERA in the majors

Johnson's electric arsenal consists of a high-90s four-seam fastball and a power slider. He has struggled to limit the walks, making him a natural fit for this walk-happy pitching staff. If the A's can harness his stuff and help him throw more strikes, he could emerge as a late-inning weapon for this bullpen-needy club.

The Green and Gold could have made more of an impact had starting catcher Shea Langeliers not suffered a torn meniscus. Given his multiple years of team control and elite all-around performance, Langeliers would have fetched the Athletics a return on par if not bigger than what the Boston Red Sox sent to the Baltimore Orioles in exchange for mutli-time All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman.

Unfortunately, Langeliers' potential season-ending injury took him off the market. It also likely contributed to the team keeping fellow catcher Jonah Heim, a free-agent at season's end.

title: MLB trade deadline winners and losers: Dodgers, Cubs and Padres all go big, while the Mets sell nearly a third of their roster
description: The Los Angeles Dodgers now have Tarik Skubal. The Boston Red Sox now have Adley Rutschman. The New York Mets now have a fully open calendar for October.
fullText:
Another MLB trade deadline has come and gone, with every contender in MLB making some sort of addition at the expense of the teams embracing reality.

It will be a long time before we understand the full ramifications of these trades due to the volatility of prospects, but no day on the MLB calendar shows which way the wind is blowing more than deadline day.

The Los Angeles Dodgers now have Tarik Skubal. The Boston Red Sox now have Adley Rutschman. The New York Mets now have a fully open calendar for October.

Let's dive into what all of this means, starting with the team that will be the talk of baseball well beyond the 2026 season.

If the Detroit Tigers were going to admit defeat and trade Tarik Skubal, the Dodgers loomed as the inevitable destination. And not for a boorish "The Dodgers get EVERYBODY!" reason.

There were basically four, maybe five teams good enough this season to justify giving up the price of two top-100 prospects and more that the Dodgers paid: the Dodgers, the Milwaukee Brewers, the Atlanta Braves, the Tampa Bay Rays and maybe the New York Yankees or Red Sox. Of that group, only the Dodgers, Brewers and Rays really had the prospect depth to make the deal happen.

The thing is, though, the Brewers and Rays usually need those prospects in a way the Dodgers don't. Those teams build their contenders via affordable pre-arb and arbitration talent, with free agency as an occasional indulgence. Meanwhile, Zyhir Hope, the crown jewel of the Dodgers' prospect package was — and we're not joking here — the third-best outfielder on L.A.'s Double-A team, according to most prospect rankings, behind Josue De Paula and Mike Sirota.

All of that left the Dodgers without another legitimate suitor to compete against. They paid a completely reasonable (but still considerable for a rental) price, Hope and two high-risk, high-reward pitchers in River Ryan and Brady Smith, in exchange for maybe the one guy available at the deadline who could have meaningfully improved their World Series odds.

They didn't stop there, either. Despite a comically large rotation depth chart, especially with Eric Lauer and Emmet Sheehan not being traded, L.A. still went for Royals starter Kris Bubic, a 2025 All-Star who is currently on the injured list but could be useful down the line.

And with Will Smith and Dalton Rushing both now on the injured list, the Dodgers brought in familiar faces Ben Rortvedt and Hunter Feduccia, who can at least offer an improvement on their worst-case scenario at the position.

No organization in all of sports combines resources, competence and the urge to bathe in the blood of your enemies quite like Andrew Friedman's front office. It was no different at this year's trade deadline.

The Dodgers might have made the biggest splash, but the crown for most total value added at this year's deadline belongs to the Cubs, who overhauled a rotation that badly need overhauling.

The team had already acquired David Peterson from the New York Mets, and the left-hander has been more than solid outside of a bizarre meltdown early last month. Then they got Kevin Gasuman from the Toronto Blue Jays, Clay Holmes from the New York Mets and Braxton Garrett from the Miami Marlins.

Gausman should offer instant impact. Holmes was the Mets' most reliable starting pitcher before he fractured his right fibula in May, but his return from the injured list is imminent. Garrett has looked promising in the past, though he's still trying to find his footing after undergoing internal brace surgery in 2024.

Chicago also landed reliever Ryan Zeferjahn from the Los Angeles Angels and outfielder Tyrone Taylor from the Mets, filling two other notable needs.

This team is definitely better than it was a couple of days ago, and it wasn't cheap, with top-100 prospects Jefferson Rojas and Moisés Ballesteros among the several prospects leaving the organization. It probably won't be enough to nullify the Brewers' 6.5-game lead in the NL Central, but this squad suddenly looks like by far the best wild-card team in the NL.

Never change, A.J. Preller. We really do mean that.

For the past few years, the San Diego Padres have been seeing the bill come due. They once had one of the most enviable collections of young talent in baseball (maybe the most enviable other than their neighbors to the slight north), but that has deteriorated through a series of win-now trades.

Now, the Padres sit at 58-54 entering play Monday, which is a vast improvement on where they were 10 games ago, and they're one game out of a competitive wild-card race. They have a minus-12 run differential. Their high-priced core is visibly aging.

So, of course, they bought again.

This time, San Diego improved a bad rotation by bringing in Robbie Ray from the San Francisco Giants and Casey Mize from the Detroit Tigers, sending away the No. 2, 4 and 9 prospects in a weak system, according to MLB Pipeline.

The Padres will remain competitive this season. They will have more questions to answer in the offseason, when top starter Michael King likely opts out and Ray and Adrian Morejon hit free agency.

That's for future Preller — or, and we say this ominously, someone else — to figure out.

It's refreshing to see a Pirates team try, even from 3.5 games out of the last wild-card spot entering Monday.

Pittsburgh ranks second in MLB in runs scored and seventh in runs allowed. There's enough talent in the rotation that the bullpen was clearly the place for improvement, and improve they did.

In deals for Luke Weaver from the Mets, Kirby Yates from the Angels and Lake Bachar from the Marlins, the Pirates bought as hard in the bullpen as any team at the deadline this year.

This is still a team with holes, and one that definitely needs to pray Paul Skenes' recent velocity issues are a temporary nuisance. And yet, this is now Pittsburgh's best chance in years to end a decade-plus playoff drought.

Remember when we said there were four or five teams good enough to have reason to acquire Skubal? Let's go through what those teams did.

The Dodgers obviously did a lot. The Brewers added rotation help with Dustin May and bullpen help with Antonio Senzatela and JoJo Romero. The Rays added a much-needed catcher in Liam Hicks and a classic reclamation project in former All-Star starter Freddy Peralta. The Yankees got some real bats in Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos. The Boston Red Sox went for it with the Rutschman blockbuster (more on that later).

The Braves, meanwhile, have a haul headlined by fourth outfielder Lane Thomas. They got a salary dump in Tyler Mahle and minor-league depth in Bailey Falter. They got Brent Suter and Tyler Uberstine, relievers who hardly scream "confident innings in October."

The Braves overall have been excellent this season. Only the Dodgers have better odds to win their division than Atlanta. But, uh, what's the plan once you're facing the Dodgers and their gatling gun of multi-million-dollar arms?

The answer to that can't be "well, the Dodgers are going to win anyway," like some fans will say. Fire any executive who says that. Success is fleeting in MLB, and you can't treat a 100% playoff team like a bonsai tree, making only the most delicate of tweaks, while all the other heavy hitters slam the buy button.

Atlanta obviously isn't done for, but there's no way to describe this deadline as anything better than a disappointment for president of baseball operations Alex Anthopolous.

The Red Sox are going for it! It is legitimately thrilling to see a team go from dead in the water to one of the deadline's biggest buyers, even if Boston's second-biggest acquisition, infielder Curtis Mead, immediately fractured his wrist.

But let's talk about that Rutschman deal.

Rutschman isn't quite the superstar he looked like he would be when he first reached MLB, but he's still one of the game's better catchers and under team control for 2027 too. Boston is probably going to love him.

As for the price general manager Craig Breslow paid for him, let's go to a talent evaluator quoted by Sean McAdam of MassLive.com: "I'm absolutely dumbfounded by this...This is literally one of the most ridiculous trades I've seen in 30 years."

In exchange for a season and a half of their new catcher plus another catcher in Jake Rogers, Boston sent away pitching prospect Anthony Eyanson (their No. 2 prospect at MLB Pipelin), pitching prospect Kyson Witherspoon (No. 4), outfield prospect Enddy Azocar (No. 5), current back-up catcher Carlos Narváez and a player to be named later.

The baseball world is prone to overrating the value of prospects, but that's still a considerable price for a guy whose median outcome is a quality starter and not much more.

Yes, we just talked about what a haul the Orioles got for Rutschman. It was a good deal, but also one that showed all the bad building up under the supposed mastermind in Baltimore.

Remember 2023? The Orioles won 101 games, they still had the best farm system in baseball, they were about to get a new owner in David Rubenstein who was supposedly willing to spend in a way the Angelos family never did. And at the center of it all was Mike Elias, the former Astros player development lead who was demonstrating the power of alchemy in Baltimore.

What happened next might be the most stark example of a would-be contender failing to take a step forward in recent memory. The Orioles never had the pitching to back up their enviable collection of hitting talent, and then all that hitting talent collectively took a step backward. They went from 101 wins in 2023 to 91 in 2024 to 75 in 2025. They are on pace for 78 wins in 2026, with a farm system that was middling before that infusion of talent from Boston.

The Rutschman trade represents the final stretch of a cycle. Elias appeared incredibly adept at the first part of the cycle, building up talent without having to care about the results on the field. He proved disastrous at the next leg, waiting for a contender to assemble itself in front of him. And now he's sending away the vanguard of that first wave of talent for fuel for the next lap.

There is little evidence the next ride will be any different, but at least Elias is doing what he loves again.

Moving back to the Dodgers, not everyone in that building will have reason to be pleased with what they've done.

Consider the case of Justin Wrobleski, who has been a pleasant surprise in his first year as an MLB starting pitcher. He entered Monday ranked 11th in MLB in ERA while ranking behind only Yoshinobu Yamamoto in innings pitched for the Dodgers. He made his first-team All-Star team last month, and would be one of the most valuable components of nearly any other MLB organization.

He is also likely to be pitching out of the bullpen this postseason if everyone is healthy. As is Roki Sasaki, who is suddenly fulfilling his potential as one of the most-hyped pitching prospects in MLB history. The Dodgers are undefeated in nine appearances by Lauer and he is one injured list return from falling out of this rotation. Sheehan got optioned like 10 minutes after the trade deadline.

In an organization with Skubal, Yamamoto, Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, it's not enough to be good for a season. We're just not sure how any young pitcher is supposed to accomplish more than that in this monstrosity of an organization.

We didn't really expect anything different, but the New York Mets have officially pulled the plug on the most disappointing season in MLB.

With Holmes, Peralta, Taylor, Weaver, Huascar Brazobán, Brooks Raley, A.J. Minter and Rortvedt, the Mets traded away eight players over the past two days. That is 31% of an MLB roster. They got back some decent talent overall, but that's not the win they wanted this season.

It's not a full rebuild in New York, but it's at the very least a moment for reflection. This team was supposed to be Dodgers East with David Stearns running the show with a near-unlimited checkbook, but little has gone right since their magical playoff run in 2024.

title: Best pitching rotations in MLB: Where Dodgers' group led by Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto ranks

title: MLB trade deadline: Giants trade 2B Luis Arraez to Phillies
description: Arraez, who signed a one-year deal with San Francisco last offseason, has bounced back with one of the best batting averages in baseball.
fullText:
Luis Arraez has found a new home, with the San Francisco Giants trading the infielder to the Philadelphia Phillies on MLB trade deadline day, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan. Right-hander Kaleb Kilian is also part of the deal. The Giants' return includes the Phillies' No. 4 prospect per MLB Pipeline, RHP Ramon Marquez, and RHP Marty Gair, according to MLB.com's Mark Feinsand.

Arraez signed a one-year, $12 million deal with San Francisco in January after a surprisingly weak free agency this offseason. But Arraez has done well with the Giants, and his production has ticked back up this season, making him one of the likely players to get dealt ahead of the deadline.

After a middling year with the San Diego Padres in 2025, Arraez is on track for a career-best season coming out of the All-Star break. Though the infielder is sometimes criticized for not having a lot of power on offense, his batting average is one of the best in baseball.

Arraez also has value as a defender, starting at second base with the Giants after being shunted to first base last year with the Padres.

The Giants are one of the bleakest teams in the league this season. Though they don't have the worst record in MLB — that honor is being passed between the Colorado Rockies and the Los Angeles Angels — San Francisco is down near the bottom, and doesn't have a lot of direction.

Arraez has been the sole bright spot for the Giants on an otherwise mediocre team. Unfortunately for fans, that meant he was the best asset for general manager Buster Posey to trade away as San Francisco looks ahead to next season.

title: Blue Jays reportedly trade Kevin Gausman to Cubs, signaling sell-off months after World Series appearance
description: The deal in part signals a Blue Jays selloff at the MLB trade deadline, months after they took the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7 of the World Series.
fullText:
The Toronto Blue Jays have traded starting pitcher Kevin Gausman to the Chicago Cubs, signaling a sell-off at the MLB trade deadline months after they took the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7 of the World Series.

The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Mitch Bannon reported the trade on Sunday, hours before Monday's 6 p.m. ET trade deadline. In return, according to the report, the Blue Jays will receive outfielder Brett Bateman and infielder Ty Southisene, both prospects.

The move in part cements a season of disappointment for the Blue Jays, who started 2026 with hopes of competing for the AL East title and returning to the postseason. Instead, they've entered the stretch run in last place in the division at 52-60 with long-shot hopes of competing for a wild-card spot.

Whether the Blue Jays would be sellers at the deadline or hold steady for a shot at the postseason was unclear before the All-Star break. But they lost five of their first six games coming out of the break, including three to the AL East-leading Tampa Bay Rays.

Gausman is playing on the final season of a five-year, $110 million contract. He was a prime candidate for a deadline deal to a contending team seeking a contributor with an expiring contract.

A two-time All-Star, Gausman isn't at his peak form at 35 years old. But he's been a reliable starter for much of his career, including this season as one of MLB's leaders in starts and innings pitched.

Gausman provides the Cubs with a mid-rotation option days after they designated veteran Jameson Taillon for assignment.

Taillon, 34, was in the midst of a career-worst season with a 5.92 ERA and 25 home runs allowed. Chicago traded Taillon to Toronto in a separate deal earlier Sunday for cash considerations or a player to be named later.

Taillon pitched 76 innings for the Cubs this season, and his departure left Chicago with a hole in their rotation. Gausman, who's made 14 postseason appearances, slots in for what the Cubs hope is an upgrade for the stretch run and a likely playoff appearance.

The Cubs leave a 2-1 loss to the Yankees on Sunday at 63-49, in control of first place in the NL wild-card standings with a four-game cushion over second. They're 6.5 game behind the Brewers for first place in the NL Central.

Per MLB Pipeline, Southisene ranked as Chicago's No. 13 prospect, and Bateman rated at No. 21. Neither are in MLB Pipeline's top 100 overall prospects. They're both now building blocks for Toronto's future.

For the Blue Jays, the trade signals a different direction. Toronto fell to 52-60 with Saturday’s loss to St. Louis and entered Sunday 13.5 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East.

Rather than holding onto Gausman for another season, the Blue Jays elected to move one of their most accomplished starters and add to their future.

The full return will ultimately help determine how the trade is evaluated. For now, however, the immediate message is clear: The Cubs believe they can contend this season, and they have added one of the most established pitchers available to help them do it.

title: Take a look at Florida alumnus Christian Scott's 2026 MLB season stats
description: Take a look at how former Florida Gators and current New York Mets has performed in his second season of major league action.
fullText:
Former Florida baseball standout Christian Scott has had a strong showing during his 2026 campaign with the New York Mets so far.

Originally drafted by the Mets in the 5th round of the 2021 MLB Draft with the 142nd overall pick, the right-handed pitcher's ascent into big league ball hit a major roadblock in 2024, when he underwent a hybridized surgery that combined a traditional Tommy John ligament replacement with a stabilizing internal brace that caused him to miss all of the 2025 campaign.

Prior to his injury, Scott threw 47 1/3 innings for New York, posting an 0-3 record with a 4.56 ERA, 4.60 FIP and 1.20 WHIP while striking out 39 against 12 walks issued across that stretch for 0.4 fWAR. He had been a breakout prospect for the franchise up to that point, rising from unranked on the team's 2023 top 30 prospects list to No. 5 heading into 2024.

So far in 2026, Scott has not only picked up where he left off, he has also made some significant strides in several categories, putting up a 3-3 record with a tidy 2.99 ERA along with a solid 3.47 FIP and 1.24 WHIP over 69 1/3 innings of work for an fWAR of 1.5. While his walks per nine have regressed from 2.3 to 3.9, the Coconut Creek, Florida, native's home runs per nine have improved from 1.5 to 0.9 and strikeouts per nine have lept from 7.4 to 11.0.

According to Statcast, Scott's overall pitching run value ranks in the 63rd percentile among major league pitchers, with his fastball run value checking in the 76th percentile. His breaking ball and offspeed run values rate below average, coming in at 48th and 36th, respectively.

Scott's primary weapon is his four-seam fastball, which he employs half the time and sits just a hair above the MLB average at 95.4 mph; he also offers a cut fastball (17%) and barely used sinker (2%). His two breaking balls are a sweeper (22%) and curveball (6%), while the splitter (4%) represents his only offspeed offering.

The former Gator excels in several of Statcast's categories, checking into the 89th percentile in strikeout rate as well as his extension. Other areas where he rates higher than the average hurler are hard-hit percentage (77th), average exit velocity (74th), expected batting average (73rd) and barrel percentage (72nd), while his chase percentage (27th), walk percentage (25th) and groundball percentage (11th) land on the lower end of the scale.

The 27-year-old righty dealt with an injury this summer that shelved him on the injured list for a stint — a hip impingement that caused him to miss some time from mid to late June. Since then, he has maintained his spot in the rotation, putting up a 2.83 ERA, 2.96 FIP and 1.08 WHIP with 38 strikeouts and 11 walks over 28 2/3 innings.

Despite Scott's success this season, the Mets have floundered to a 47-65 record, landing them in the basement of the National League West division despite having the second-largest payroll in all of baseball.

Over 116 2/3 innings stretching across 24 appearances — all starts — Scott has posted a 3.63 ERA, 3.93 FIP and 1.23 WHIP for New York, amassing a 3-6 record along the way. So far, he has averaged 9.57 strikeouts against 3.24 walks per nine innings, along with 1.16 home runs per nine, and has accumulated a total of 2.0 fWAR.

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across MLB. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Dodgers fans and fans across the country. 

What do you get the team with the most talent in the sport? We asked you guys, and a new catcher was at the top of the wishlist, taking 47 percent of the votes. Before getting into what that might entail, let’s take a moment to appreciate the absurdity that not a single vote was cast for a position player (outside of catcher) — rightfully so, with no open spot on this roster the team could realistically hope to improve on That and other priorities, of course, while trying to improve its World Series odds.

The remaining 53 percent who didn’t vote for catcher were nearly split between starting and relief pitching. Both units share the exciting prospect of reinforcements on the way or recently arrived, with Edwin Díaz just activated and Blake Snell not far behind him. While any bullpen could always use an extra arm, the starting staff has this looming cloud over it with questions regarding the availability of Shohei Ohtani.

Assessing options on the market for these positions of “need,” with Will Smith’s rehab finally showing promising signs, the Dodgers may very well limit themselves to less splashy options. As we covered before here, Victor Caratini and Ryan Jeffers of the Twins may represent the best targets. A pending free agent, Jeffers wouldn’t cost a king’s ransom, unlike other more exciting controllable catchers, and the veteran Caratini would represent a safety net type of acquisition.

On the starting pitching front, with Eric Lauer thriving since being acquired by the Dodgers and Snell returning, it feels like a Tarik Skubal or bust kind of situation. Sure, there are other options who could prove to be an improvement over what the Dodgers have on the backend of the rotation right now, at least in terms of ceiling, but they’re not particularly likely moves. Unfortunately for the Dodgers, some of the better potentially available relievers at the deadline play for the Padres, making for a difficult deal as San Diego would inevitably prefer to move them to someone else. Everyone might want to talk about Mason Miller as the dream target, but pending free agent Adrian Morejón might be a more feasible acquisition and a great one in his own right.

Whether the target is a starter or a reliever, perhaps the best team to talk with is the Mets. While their record is atrocious, the Mets don’t lack in high-end reliever quality, with Brooks Raley and Luke Weaver pitching great and firmly available. A.J. Minter was also in this group, but he was the first to go, traded to the Twins on Thursday night. In the unlikely scenario the Dodgers want to add a starter not named Skubal, Clay Holmes ticks a lot of boxes, having recently returned from an injury and heading for the open market at the end of the year.

title: MLB trade deadline: Latest rumors on Tarik Skubal, Hunter Greene, and more
description: What are the latest rumors ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline?
fullText:
If you believe Jeff Passan, today is the day we will start seeing trades ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline, which arrives Monday.

So let’s spin around the rumors again.

Wednesday afternoon, Tarik Skubal exited the Detroit Tigers’ game against the Baltimore Orioles in the top of the seventh, having given up a two-run single. He left to a standing ovation from the Detroit faithful, who were wondering like the rest of us whether it was his last outing for the Tigers. He exited having handed the Detroit bullpen a 7-1 lead with two outs and a pair of runners aboard.

What happened after that is, according to one MLB executive, the final “sign” that the Tigers need to move their ace at the deadline.

Baltimore scored four more runs in the inning, and went on to win 10-9 in extras. Despite recording his 1,000th strikeout in the performance, Skubal received a no-decision for his efforts.

“If there was ever a sign that the Tigers should trade Skubal, that was it. The offers should start flowing in any minute,” said one NL executive to MLB insider Mark Feinsand.

Feinsand was not the only one reporting that a deal would be happening. ESPN’s Jeff Passan declared Skubal “will be traded” in his MLB Trade Deadline preview as well.

So what teams could be making a move for the ace? As we outlined yesterday the Milwaukee Brewers are among the suitors, and Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that the Chicago Cubs are expected to make a run at the left-hander. But according to Passan, when it comes to potential suitors they are “all almost resigned to the idea that the Los Angeles Dodgers are going to get Tarik Skubal.”

A potential reason for that? The lingering health issues for Shohei Ohtani. With the superstar dealing with left knee and right bicep issues, it has put his time on the bump on hold. His last start came on July 3, and manager Dave Roberts indicated earlier this week that his throwing program is on hold. “Trying to mitigate that, we stopped the throwing, stopped the bullpens — hopefully, No. 1, take care of the knee and then not have him try to create velocity with the arm that’s not 100%,” Roberts said.

With Ohtani on the shelf — as a pitcher — that could mean a big push for Skubal from the Dodgers.

If you’re looking for a sleeper team in the Skubal sweepstakes, keep an eye on Tampa Bay. The Rays saw left-hander Shane McClanahan leave his start on Thursday with “back tightness,” and while it is not considered a “long-term” issue, there is an opening for Tampa Bay. As one MLB source told MLB.com, “[t]he Brewers, Rays and Dodgers have the most high-end prospects to move. It would be somewhat surprising if he didn’t wind up with one of those three teams.”

While Skubal will command the headlines, another top arm could be on the move.

According to MLB.com, there is a “50-50” chance that the Cincinnati Reds move flame-thrower Hunter Greene ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline. Greene missed the first half of the season following surgery to remove bone chips from his right elbow, as he put off the surgery last season and threw through the discomfort, option for an injection rather than surgery.

He ultimately went under the knife in the spring, costing him the start to 2026. Since returning he has gone 2-2 with a 7.06 ERA in four starts this season.

But this is a former All-Star, who is under club control for the next few seasons. He signed a six-year extension with Cincinnati in 2023, and is controlled through 2028. Greene is owed $15 million in 2027, $16 million in 2028, and has a $21 million club option for 2029, and his contract comes with a $2 million buyout.

His health is probably the biggest concern, as he has missed time beyond the recent surgery. Tommy John surgery in 2018 cost him the entire 2019 Minor League campaign, and he has lost time due to shoulder and lower-body issues.

“Health,” said one MLB executive to MLB.com about the concern. “He falls into the high quality and moderate-to-low quantity category.”

Still, during his 2024 All-Star campaign, he went 9-5 with a 2.75 ERA, earning Cy Young votes. Teams that miss on Skubal could be enticed to bet on that talent — at that low cost — for the next few years.

Our friends at Battery Power are taking about Greene as well:

As we noted yesterday, the New York Yankees are one of several teams looking for help behind the plate at the MLB Trade Deadline.

According to longtime MLB insider Jon Heyman, the Yankees have inquired with the Baltimore Orioles about Adley Rutschman, but from the outside looking in it would seem unlikely that Mike Elias would move the catcher within the division:

Yankees are among many teams to check on 3-time All-Star/switch-hitting catcher Adley Rutschman. NYY is casting a wide net for catching need. Ryan Jeffers, pending free agent, seemed logical but Twins suggest they’re a buyer now. Tyler Stephenson, others are on NYY list

— Jon Heyman (@JonHeyman) July 29, 2026

However, Passan reported on his podcast earlier this week that the Orioles are at least “open” to moving players such as Rutschman. Open is one thing, but making a deal … and one to the Yankees … is another.

Colorado Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman is another option generating buzz, given last year’s slash line of .278/.323/.520, but the fact that he has three arbitration years coming up before he becomes a free agent in 2030 has pushed the asking price up.

With the Los Angeles Dodgers running away with things in the NL West, the San Diego Padres sit in third place, 14 games back in the division.

But at one game over .500, the Padres are just two games out in the NL Wild Card chase, so moving a key player ahead of hte deadline does not seem likely.

Until you remember general manager A.J. Preller is involved

After swinging last year’s biggest move, the deal with the Athletics for closer Mason Miller, could Preller really turn around and trade him at the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline? According to Passan it is at least possible, but Preller has been telling teams that no prospect can be listed as off limits in such a deal.

With the New York Mets mired at the bottom of the NL standings, they are expected to move some players ahead of the deadline.

One of them could be right-hander Clay Holmes.

Holmes has not pitched in the majors since mid-May, when he suffered a broken right fibula, but was 4-4 in his nine starts with a 2.39 ERA and WHIP of 1.101. He is set to hit free agency at the end of the season, but is still expected to have a “strong” market. One AL executive told FanSided that “[i]t would be a surprise if he didn’t [get traded].”

title: TRADE: Tigers Deal 7-Year MLB Veteran Catcher for 24-Year-Old Pitcher

The Baltimore Orioles acquired catcher Jake Rogers from the Detroit Tigers on Thursday for minor league right-hander Zane Barnhart, ending Rogers’ seven-year run in Detroit.

Baltimore has been sending journeymen behind the plate for nearly two weeks with Adley Rutschman and Samuel Basallo both on the injured list, and the trade deadline arrives Monday.

Rogers never reached waivers. Detroit designated him for assignment on July 28 to clear a roster spot for Javier BÃ¡ez, back from the high ankle sprain that cost him three months. The Tigers found a taker inside 48 hours.

Rogers debuted for Detroit on July 30, 2019, exactly seven years before the trade that ended his time there. He had come over in the deal that sent Justin Verlander to the Houston Astros in August 2017, and he was the last player from that trade still in the organization, as noted by Bless You Boys.

Rogers missed all of 2022 with an injury.

Rutschman went on the injured list July 20 with left wrist inflammation, his third IL stint of the season after left ankle trouble in April and a concussion in June, Rich Dubroff of BaltimoreBaseball.com reported. Basallo followed two days later with right shoulder inflammation.

That left Sam Huff and Chadwick Tromp. Baltimore then claimed Yohel Pozo off waivers from the St. Louis Cardinals and designated Huff, a move detailed by the Baltimore Sun. Huff was hitting .121. The Orioles sat 53-56, close enough to the wild card to keep buying, as MLB.com‘s Jake Rill reported Sunday.

Rogers gives manager Craig Albernaz a catcher who has worked 362 major league games, including Tarik Skubal’s starts during the left-hander’s Cy Young seasons. He has thrown out 26.7% of base stealers in 2026, though Statcast has graded his framing and blocking below average, according to MLB Trade Rumors.

The bat is another problem. Rogers is hitting .161/.266/.301 with three home runs in 34 games, and his career line sits at .197/.270/.379 with 47 homers. Rogers is earning $3.05 million this year and reaches free agency in November.

The 31-year-old was a third-round pick out of Tulane by Houston in 2016. His one big offensive season came in 2023, when he hit 21 home runs and slugged .444 across 107 games. He lost all of 2022 to elbow surgery.

Barnhart reports to Double-A Erie, according to the transaction log at CBS Sports.

The 24-year-old right-hander was born in Towson, Maryland, grew up in Medina, Ohio, and pitched at Division II Hillsdale College, where he turned himself from a two-way player into a closer and became the highest-drafted player in program history. Baltimore took him in the 17th round in 2023, 511th overall, and signed him for $100,000, according to Spotrac.

“Going into Hillsdale, I was throwing 85 miles an hour, and I got out of there throwing up to 98 my junior year. Huge leaps,” Barnhart told the Hillsdale Collegian in April.

He has worked exclusively in relief as a professional, compiling a 3.41 ERA with 167 strikeouts and a 1.24 WHIP over 150.1 innings. This season with Double-A Chesapeake he is 2-3 with a 4.05 ERA and 45 strikeouts in 40 innings over 31 appearances.

The San Francisco Giants are going to be trade deadline sellers this season, and there are plenty of interesting names worth considering at this year's deadline from the Giants' roster.

Luis Arraez and Robbie Ray are the two headliners as rental options, but Heliot Ramos is another player who could fetch some legitimate trade interest. However, the Giants might also entertain trade offers on some expensive veterans this summer.

For MLB insider Andy McCullough of The Athletic, he would be "shocked" if the Giants traded $313.5 million slugger Rafael Devers at the trade deadline for a simple reason: his contract.

"I would be absolutely shocked - shocked! - if the Giants could move Devers' contract," McCullough writes.

For as good a hitter as Devers is, posting a solid .796 OPS this season after a very slow start to the year, the Giants would be hard-pressed to find a team willing to take on his contract.

Devers is in the middle of a massive 10-year, $313.5 million contract that runs through the 2033 season. Such a large and lengthy contract is a real problem for the Giants in potential trade conversations.

MORE: Giants willing to trade Heliot Ramos in big news for many MLB clubs

Teams would likely ask the Giants to take on some of that contract to consider a trade, and if the Giants did somehow find a team willing to take on his deal, the other team probably wouldn't want to give up much in return.

The Giants are, effectively, stuck with Devers, barring some unforeseen interest from a desperate MLB team. For now, Devers is a Giant and doesn't look likely to be leaving anytime soon.

Devers would be a good trade target if he weren't so expensive, especially for someone who's a DH-only or a questionable defensive first baseman.

There is almost no chance Devers is traded now, or in the future. His $313.5 million contract is a massive hurdle to a deal, and McCullough, like the rest of the baseball world, would be "shocked" if the Giants somehow found a trade partner for Devers.

title: 2026 MLB Trade Deadline Near With Most Teams Rocking Same Parity Boat
description: The next five days will decide the future of many MLB players and teams. The trade deadline is August 3. Who knows who goes where and who doesn't by 6 p.m. ET on Monday?
fullText:
The next five days will determine the future fate of many MLB players and teams. The 2026 MLB Trade Deadline is August 3, and who goes where or stays put by 6 p.m. ET on Monday is tied to which teams win or lose until then.

There isn’t a team in any sport on any level on the planet that isn’t wishing to improve. In that sense, all 30 MLB teams would like to be “buyers” adding better and more expensive players by Monday. Some simply do not have the talent needed to exchange or the money to pay in return, however. Those clubs would usually be classified as “sellers” seeking to cut payroll and add promising prospects in hopes of rebuilding for the future.

Except that in 2026, the future could be now – given the results of the next five days. The best possible prizes, pitchers Tarik Skubal and Mason Miller and shortstop C.J. Abrams could be retained to help their teams keep winning or dealt to wave the white flag for 2026 with hopes of waving a pennant in 2027.

Each league has 12 teams reasonably in the running for one of six playoff spots apiece. Therefore, only six teams total are basically out of it and presumably more eager to be “sellers” of their best players.

Yet if those “best players” were performing real well in 2026, those clubs would not be in the predicament of essentially saying sayonara, see you next year. There’s not a high demand for the cream of the tail-end crop.

It’s a classic catch-22 scenario – which brings to mind a humorous anecdote. When asked why defensively-challenged Dick Stuart was nicknamed “Catch 22” in the 1960s, a teammate replied, “Because if you made 50 throws to him, he’d catch 22.”

The odds should be higher that the majority of MLB teams will make a player move or two by the impending deadline. Except this year, determining who goes where is tougher than usual since clubs are traditionally unwilling to deal with a team it is battling in the standings. So in 2026, perhaps we should look for more trades involving AL and NL teams.

Conversely, the “I’ll help you, since you are not in direct competition” thinking may restrict the number of trades as it curtails the number of possibilities.

It sounds undecisive, unpredictable and a bit screwy only because it is.

In 2026, the Angels, Athletics, Blue Jays, Cardinals, Giants, Mets, Rockies and Royals appear to be most likely sellers. A couple other teams could join that group this weekend.

Veteran infielder Luis Arraez is often mentioned as likely to be dealt by San Francisco despite his .326 batting average, second in the National League. The Giants (45-61) are 9.5 games out of a possible wild-card spot and Arraez is due to become an unrestricted free agent in 2027.

A contender needing offense could want the three-time batting champion who since the end of 2022 has played for Minnesota, Miami, San Diego and San Francisco. Miami’s 2024 trade of Arraez got prospects that have helped the Marlins improve.

Those needing a pitcher and willing to pay off a contract could contact Toronto about Kevin Gausman. The 35-year-old will be owed $7 million this year after the deadline. Since May 23, he is 0-7 to put his record at 4-10 as the defending AL champion Blue Jays are five games behind Cleveland for the final wild-card spot.

In his loss streak, Gausman got only 14 runs (2.0 a game) of support. So a rival GM could figure, “He is pitching well enough to win with us.”

Then again, if Toronto runs the table the next five days, the Blue Jays may be back in true contention and decide to add players. It’s that close and questionable.

Teams on the cusp of contending today could be out of it or on a winning streak by Monday. Sitting on the fence right now, contemplating various scenarios are the Marlins, Nationals, Orioles, Padres, Tigers and Twins.

That leaves 16 buyers, though a bad five days by some of them could completely change their plans.

A great stretch already altered the Boston Red Sox’ fortunes and thinking. A 15-game winning streak and 20-2 record from June 25 to July 22 took them from last place into solid playoff contention. So the Red Sox fired an “early” trade shot.

Boston made the first buyers’ salvo on July 26 by acquiring infielder Curtis Mead from Washington for pitcher Connelly Early. "This move makes our major league roster better," Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Breslow told reporters. “We think this is a move to make us better in 2026 and we’ll continue to look for these opportunities.”

Alas, Mead is out with a broken left wrist, incurred when hit by a pitch in his second time at bat for Boston.

Six clubs already have 60 or more wins with less than 60 games to play. The Los Angeles Dodgers (67 wins), Milwaukee Brewers (66), Tampa Bay Rays (62), Atlanta Braves (62), New York Yankees (60) and Chicago Cubs (60) are likely to enter a different competition in the coming days – trying to beat out each other in acquiring needed players.

The Rays are ruling the rugged AL East, helped by deadline deals of a year ago. Those that buy best now could leave others in their wake and wave bye-bye.

The Seattle Mariners did it last year by acquiring Josh Naylor and Eugenio Suarez from Arizona near the deadline. The duo combined for 22 homers, 64 RBI and 22 stolen bases (19 in 19 tries by the hefty Naylor) as Seattle went from five games back to winning the AL West.

Traditionally, the Dodgers and Yankees have both the minor-league prospect supply and revenue needed to get whoever they want. The Braves and Cubs usually are pro-active, too, while the Brewers and Rays often seek more prospects in favor of paring payroll and increasing future forecasts.

Milwaukee and Tampa Bay may jump into the foray this time. Both have minor-league systems loaded with prospects each accumulated at deadlines in recent years and could flip this time. Tampa Bay also has a new ownership group that gives the franchise the ability to put money where its’ wish list is for the first time.

It is all too topsy-turvy to predict who is going to do what within the next five days – both on the playing field and on the telephone wheeling and dealing.

Hall of Fame pitcher Satchel Paige once said, “Ain’t no man can avoid being born average, but there ain’t no man that got to be common.” He meant that men are born in parity, but can work to rise above it.

The 2026 MLB Trade Deadline gives teams – and by extension their fans – the opportunity to boldly break from current parity, go for it all, and perhaps experience the thrill of being a champion.

title: Cody Bellinger injury adds urgency to Yankees trade deadline plans
description: Cody Bellinger's Grade 2 hamstring strain adds pressure on the Yankees to upgrade before the MLB trade deadline.
fullText:
Cody Bellinger’s worse-than-expected hamstring strain adds a new layer to the Yankees’ trade deadline period.

Diagnosed on Monday with a Grade 2 left hamstring strain, Bellinger’s four-to-six week timeline to return puts him back in the Yankees’ lineup sometime in September.

But even with Bellinger, a compromised Yankees lineup – no Aaron Judge since June 2, no Giancarlo Stanton since April 25 – had become a deeper issue.

Before their 9-5 win against the White Sox on Monday night, the second-place Yankees were 14-19 since June 19, averaging 3.27 runs per game.

Prior to that, the Yankees were averaging 5.27 runs per game and leading the AL East by 3.5 games.

Of course, every pinstriped hope of a deep October run is connected to Judge’s return.

And we’re still waiting on the second re-imaging of Judge’s fractured first right rib, and for his clearance just to begin baseball activity.

With Stanton, the constant he’s-getting-closer narrative should never limit the pursuit of more offense.

Still, impact bats are tough to find in this trade market, and you wonder about the appeal for the Yanks to absorb a bad contract or another DH-only type.

In recent days, potential offensive targets in Cincinnati’s Spencer Steer (wrist), San Francisco’s Casey Schmitt (knee) and even A’s catcher Shea Langeliers (knee), a longshot trade candidate, have receded due to injury.

A right-handed hitting outfielder is a better Yankee fit, and Kansas City has two impending free agents in Starling Marte and Lane Thomas. And the Mets' Tyrone Taylor is an increasingly intriguing option.

Elsewhere, if the Tigers choose to trade lefty ace Tarik Skubal, might they also be inclined to deal fellow impending free agent Gleyber Torres?

But the defensive fit in the Bronx is an issue, which also applies to Padres’ lefty-hitting second baseman Luis Arraez, also in his free agent walk year.

Still, the Bellinger situation doesn’t alter the Yanks’ top areas to upgrade.

The search for a swing-and-miss reliever and a right-handed hitting catcher could take the Yankees right up to Monday’s MLB trade deadline.

With an .856 OPS in nine games since his return from a left hamate bone fracture, right-handed hitting Minnesota catcher Ryan Jeffers – an impending free agent – is one possible target.

But the Twins are also three games back in the middling AL Central and one game behind for the last AL wild card spot entering Tuesday, so Jeffers’ trade status remains an interesting case.

And if there’s one huge trade to be made this deadline period, San Diego closer Mason Miller is the all-in candidate, with monumental end-game impact and team control through 2029.

If the Padres are inclined, lefty reliever Adrian Morejon – a free agent after this season – is a solid trade candidate. Plus, the Yanks’ past solid relationships with Luke Weaver and the rehabbing Clay Holmes (leg fracture) puts the Mets in play as a potential trade partner.

Bellinger’s absence further weakens the Yankees defensively, an overall area that needs to be addressed.

With appreciation of his utility value, Max Schuemann is an infielder playing out of position in left field, where Bellinger’s 19 defensive runs saved this year has boosted one of the league’s best pitching staffs.

For all his hard work and leadership, Amed Rosario is a liability at any defensive position, and he’s been less of a lefty masher this year, batting .197 overall in his last 25 games.

Top Yankees’ prospect George Lombard Jr. has initially struggled to hit each time he’s moved up a level, and you’d be asking a lot for him to debut in a pennant race.

But his plus-defensive skills at shortstop make him a prime candidate for an August call-up, as one more way to bolster the club’s pitching – its primary strength.

At last year’s deadline, the Yankees became a much better team down the stretch, in part, because of third baseman Ryan McMahon’s defensive presence.

Lombard could have that kind of impact even if he bats .208, which was McMahon’s average in 54 games after his arrival last summer from Colorado.

title: Why the Tigers should (and shouldn't) trade star ace Tarik Skubal at the 2026 MLB trade deadline
description: The Tigers have a decision to make on Tarik Skubal. Here's what they will have to consider.
fullText:
Why the Tigers should (and shouldn't) trade star ace Tarik Skubal at the 2026 MLB trade deadline originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Every contender is looking for an upgrade ahead of the MLB trade deadline, but no player might be more coveted than Tigers ace Tarik Skubal.

The two-time Cy Young Award winner is a pending free agent and has been viewed as a trade candidate since the Tigers fell as many as 16 games under .500 early in the season.

With better results in recent weeks, however, Detroit could still hold on to Skubal and try to make another run at the postseason.

What's the right decision? Here are the cases for and against the Tigers trading Skubal.

MORE:16 players who could be traded by MLB deadline

Barring a drastic change of heart, the Tigers aren't going to re-sign Skubal. The two sides have reportedly remained far apart in contract talks, and the record-setting $13 million gap between Skubal and the Tigers during the arbitration process was likely the final nail in the coffin.

With that in mind, if the Tigers held on to Skubal for the remainder of the season, what would it take to make that decision a success? If it's strictly a World Series win, you can probably take that idea off the table. Not only are the Tigers still comfortably under .500, but there isn't any reason to believe they have the talent to win a championship.

Is it a trip to the World Series? The American League is wide open, but if the Tigers couldn't get past the ALDS last season, that's hard to envision. If the ALCS, which is also unlikely, would justify keeping Skubal, Detroit should think long and hard about whether that's a worthwhile goal.

From a practical standpoint, making the postseason is unlikely. The Tigers are facing a six-game deficit in the AL Central, which is manageable, but they have three teams ahead of them rather than just one team to chase down. Detroit is closer in the wild-card race but faces the same dynamic, with four teams separating the franchise from the final wild-card team.

Skubal is coming off two excellent starts, his best since returning from the injured list. If he isn't coming back next season, it makes more sense to go get some value instead of holding on to a pipe dream of a magical October run.

MORE:Tarik Skubal makes trade deadline stance clear

The Tigers might not want their reputation to be that of a team that had a chance at the postseason and threw it away by dealing a beloved ace. With the American League so mediocre and the final wild-card team hovering near .500, Detroit could set a goal of 83-85 wins and enter a wild-card series with one of baseball's elite pitchers setting the tone in Game 1.

Looking around the AL, only two teams are more than six games over .500: the Rays, who still have to prove that they can win in October, and the Yankees, who have held their own in the second half but are struggling to find any offense with Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton and now Cody Bellinger injured.

The Tigers may see 2026 as their year to make a run in October — if they can get there. Getting there with Skubal is challenging. Getting there without Skubal is just about impossible.

The value Detroit would have been able to get for Skubal earlier in his contract would have been immense, but the value for him as a rental might not be enough to totally transform the organization. If that's the case, the Tigers can show their fans that they aren't willing to quit on the season and give this group a real chance to make a push.

MORE: Every Cy Young winner in the history of the award

Skubal is set to be a free agent after this season. The Tigers ace is making $32 million after the salary arbitration process ruled in his favor over Detroit's significantly lower $19 million offer.

That gap has convinced most fans that Skubal is headed elsewhere in free agency in the winter, and Skubal recently made comments that alluded to some lingering tension between himself and the front office.

If the Tigers decide their best bet is to keep Skubal and try to engineer a miraculous postseason run, they run the risk of getting no talent back for one of the best pitchers in baseball, much like the Angels when they held onto Shohei Ohtani at the 2023 deadline.
